Built on the proven leadership principles of Coach Pat Summitt, the program equips individuals to take ownership, communicate more effectively and strengthen trust within their team.

Lesson 1 of 7
The Power of Team

(Download the transcript below)

Heading

We live in the era of entrepreneurship, the solo enterprise, the gig economy, the individual contributor, etc. There’s been a shift over the last five to 10 years that places a premium on individual autonomy and flexibility. Workplaces are scrambling to catch up with this new normal, including retention of their current team members.

But going it solo can be a lonely place! While some thrive on it, others are forsaking the world of freelance and contractorship only to re-plug into the dynamic of a team. Many employees never left in the first place and are wondering if their current environment can hold up to the ideals of culture, loyalty, and sense of shared accomplishment that we all crave when we join a company.

Pat Summitt was no stranger to the power of team. Not only did she excel in taking freshmen athletes from vastly different backgrounds and turning them into well-oiled championship machines, she went beyond the traditional requirements of a functioning team with her infamous Definite Dozen. Coach Summitt embraced these unique principles as the 12 requirements for success in any organization, including the teams she coached.

As we learned in the previous course, all 12 of these principles are important. But now it’s time to take a closer look at one of the bedrocks of the modern workforce that seems to erode with each passing year — one that is still vital to a well-oiled organization and the overall health and satisfaction of those who work there: The Power of Team.

video.transcript_text:
Introduction: The Power of Team 
Joan Cronan 
Did you grow up in a high-functioning team? Some people learn the power of teamwork 
through their high school sports. For some, the concept of team is new in the workforce. Still, 
others may have experienced the concept of team before, but a slightly dysfunctional one. 
Wherever you're starting from, the power of team in today's workforce isn't a skill that comes 
naturally. To say so much emphasis placed on honing individuals or subject matter expertise 
that qualities that become a world-class team often fade to the background. 
Pat Summitt was no stranger to the importance of team, and she was a social engineer at 
building championship-level performing teams. That included individuals from all walks of life. 
Pat once said, "Team building starts by recruiting good people and turning them into willing 
role models early on." 
How do you convince a group of highly talented individual performers to set aside their 
personal feelings, ambitions, and agendas in favor of a united effort? When I think about this 
and I think about Pat, I often think about what she thought was so important was people 
knowing their role. I remember one year we had three seniors on the team. All of them were 
great players. We had a freshman who was really better than the three seniors. And it came 
time to vote for All-American. Pat came in and said, "I need to vote for the freshman, but I hate 
to leave these two seniors who've had a great year off." And I said, "Let's talk about it." And she 
said, "I need to talk to them." So, she went in and she talked to them about why she was going 
to vote for the freshman and why the other two were such an important part of the team. 
Guess what? We went on into the championship. One of the seniors got the most valuable 
player at the SEC tournament. The next senior got the most valuable player at the regionals. 
And the freshman helped us win a national championship and was an All-American. That might 
not have happened if Pat didn't realize the importance of team and how it affected everybody 
else. 
Communication and the roles that they play are so important. In this program, we'll identify 
some important characteristics for building a great team wherever you are. We'll take a closer 
look specifically at Pat's Definite Dozen of loyalty, responsibility, and communication, three of 
the core principles for forming a healthy, functioning group. At the end of each lesson, you'll be 
challenged to build on these principles with personal reflections and short exercises. At the end 
of each module, there is a short quiz to test what you've learned. At the end of this course, 
you'll know more about teamwork and the key components that can take your teams to the 
next level. Let's get started.

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 2 of 7
Why Is Team Important?

Why Is the Concept of Team More Important Than Ever?

You’ve heard the old saying, “People don’t leave jobs, they leave leaders.” It could equally be said that people don’t leave missions, they leave dysfunctional teams.
Show me a person who is healthy, functional, plugged in to an organization’s overall mission — someone who truly enjoys working with their fellow team members and feels valued by the organization — and I’ll show you someone who is harder to entice away for a few thousand dollars more per year. These people aren’t even looking elsewhere. It’s the team member who feels isolated, undervalued, and disconnected from the overall mission who is looking over the fence for greener pastures.

So how do you build great teams? Pat would be the first to tell us that people aren’t born great team players. “Teamwork does not come naturally,” she once noted. “How do you convince a group of highly talented individual performers to set aside their personal feelings, ambitions, and agendas in favor of a unified effort?”1 As a coach, it was a problem she personally faced on an annual basis.

Teamwork does not come naturally. How do you convince a group of highly talented individual performers to set aside their personal feelings, ambitions, and agendas in favor of a unified effort?”

Click to hear the above quote.

The truth is, not everyone grew up playing sports where we were taught the power of team. It’s not a skill you necessarily learn in school, as academic performance is up to one’s individual efforts. By contrast, some people grew up playing on dysfunctional teams or participating in extracurricular activities where there were only one or two stars and everyone else on the team was merely an accessory. Yet, if people were honest, it’s the very thing most of us crave — to join with others in pursuit of a healthy, fulfilling mission.

Lesson 4 of 7
Team Involves More Than Output

The Concept of Team Involves More Than Output

The goal of Pat’s championship programs wasn’t to develop star players; it was to have an unbeatable team year after year. “Team-building starts by recruiting good people and turning them into willing role players early on,” she taught.
Self-discipline, responsibility, hard work, and individual performance may come naturally to some, but how do you teach shared ownership, respect for others, loyalty, good communication, respect for the leader, and no gossip, just to name a few?
While all the Definite Dozen principles are important, there are three principles in particular whose lack arguably causes a majority of the problems for teams in the modern workforce.

Click to expand and complete this element.

Responsibility

How do you encourage your employees to take ownership for their work and embrace/internalize the shared vision of the company?

Loyalty

How do you cultivate employees who are loyal to the company and its mission?

Communication

Organizations move at the speed of communication and trust. How do you foster team communication — from the top down, from the bottom up, and from side-to-side among peers?

There’s a reason these are principles #2 to #4 on the Definite Dozen(c) wheel. We’ll call them the LCR (Loyalty, Communication, Responsibility) of team-building.

Team-building starts by recruiting good people and turning them into willing role players early on.”

Lesson 6 of 7
Learning to Master LCR

How Do You Develop Winning Teams by Mastering LCR?

In the upcoming modules, we’ll take a closer look at these three Summitt principles, specifically:

How to encourage responsibility in your team members

How to take responsibility for your area (without micromanaging)

How to be an excellent communicator

The right balance of positive/negative communication

How to show loyalty to your team

How to be a leader employees will never want to leave

And more!

Heading

But first, let’s take a look at some reflections and exercises around the concept of team.

This course also comes with a downloadable workbook. Refer to your workbook for the personal reflection questions and exercises at the end of each lesson.

Lesson 7 of 7
Personal Reflections

Refer to these questions in your workbook. Take a minute to sit down and assess your starting point. Where are you currently as a team and as a leader?

Who are the key players on your organizational team?

On a scale of 1 to 10, how well do you think they currently pull together as a team:

What are some of the team’s areas of strength?What are areas of team weakness?

Of the LCR principles, in which area is your team the strongest?

Who is the person on your team who seems the most natural in their role? List up to three. Which team members need more development? List up to three.

How well do you know your team outside of work: birthdays, hobbies, families, favorite sports teams, etc.
1 ----------------------------------------------- 5 ------------------------------------------------ 10
Not very well                                       Somewhat                                             Pretty well

Exercises

When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

What are your three biggest obstacles or questions around the concept of team?

How would you like to grow more as the leader of the team? Take five minutes and jot your thoughts in your workbook.

Sources:

Lesson 1 of 5
The Big Chair

If you don’t want responsibility, don’t sit in the big chair.”

(Download the transcript below)

Heading

In Reach for the Summitt, Coach Summitt is famous for saying, “If you don’t want responsibility, don’t sit in the big chair.”1 Whether it’s a corner office, an executive board room, or a mere cubicle away from the people you manage, “the big chair” comes in all shapes and sizes nowadays.

“Here’s part two,” Pat admonished. “The most successful you are, the more responsibility you must assume. Responsibility never ends… you don’t finish it and move on to something more interesting. Responsibility is a constant state of being.”

“You want to talk about responsibility, let’s talk about [college] kids,” she quipped. “You really want to talk about responsibility, let’s talk about being in charge of 12 kids at a time, a dozen young women from all over the country, each with their own varying dispositions, backgrounds, problems, quarrels, and love interests. Some of them with cars.”

Pat once famously told a story about her friends deciding to throw her a 16th birthday party at a country club in Ashland City when she was in high school. Thrilled, she told her dad she needed the day off from her chores around the farm, but he told her she couldn’t go because they needed to load hay bales.
“I spent that birthday sitting on the tractor. There were about 1,000 bales of hay that needed loading,” she recalled. “My father’s point was, you can’t pick and choose the days you feel like being responsible. It’s not something that disappears when you’re tired.”

You can’t pick and choose the days you feel like being responsible. It’s not something that disappears when you’re tired."

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 1: The Big Chair 
Dr. Roberto Fernandez-Romero 
Ah, responsibility. It's a word you've heard over and over and over again. If you're watching 
this video, chances are you know a thing or two about responsibility at your organization. 
Pat believed responsibility was key to having success as a leader. Not just personal 
success, but going beyond that to instill a sense of responsibility in your team. Easier said 
than done, right? There are certain steps to walking through this art of cultivating 
responsibility, which we'll get to in a moment. 
But first, take a minute to think about where you are at your organization. In what areas 
does responsibility come most naturally? In what areas do you wish you could step up your 
own responsibility or encourage a little more responsibility among your team members? 
Even more important, what could your group accomplish if everyone understood the 
concept of being responsible? Not only for the output in their area, but the shared mission 
of the team. Pat believed a few simple principles were necessary when it comes to being a 
leader. 
You have to have responsibility for everything. If the ship is on fire, it's your responsibility. If 
the boat doesn't have enough gas, it's your responsibility. If the team didn't bring enough 
snacks for the trip, it's your responsibility.  
You have to instill responsibility in your team. As a leader, you can't go around shouldering 
100% of the burden. Not if you want to be able to lead effectively and grow a capable team 
underneath you. They, too, must have levels of responsibility and tasks they are uniquely 
accountable for. You have to look for intentional ways to encourage responsibility on your 
team. 
That brings us to the last point. You have to clearly define who is responsible for what. And 
you have to actively cultivate different levels of responsibility. 
Pat believed in starting small and working team members into greater levels of 
accountability. Everyone on the team had things they were accountable for, with no one 
being a spectator. We'll explore these concepts and more in the following lessons.

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 3 of 5
Sitting in the Chair

Sitting in the Chair

In a nutshell, Pat believed that to have responsibility and overall success as a leader, you had to consider these main elements.
(Scroll through to complete this element)

Conclusion:

Consider how you can implement these main points with your team in order to cultivate increasing levels of responsibility.

You have to have responsibility. For everything.

Pat’s message was simple: You have to have responsibility. For everything. “To be successful, you must accept full responsibility,” she said. “For everything. Headaches, problems, crises. Even when it doesn’t seem fair.”

You have to instill responsibility in your team.

Pat believed the best way to do this was bit by bit, one task at a time, rather than projecting a lot of responsibility on one person overnight. At the University of Tennessee, she famously increased her players’ responsibilities to each other slowly and incrementally over four years. By the time each player was a senior, they were assigned mentoring roles and had personal charge of an incoming freshman.

You have to clearly define who is responsible for what.

“I must make sure that the responsibilities of our players and staff are clearly delineated and that everyone understands them. That way, when there is a breakdown, we know what happened,” Pat once said. If you don’t know who is responsible for what, when there’s a problem in a particular area, you won’t know who the clear, “wringable neck” is for that area.

You have to actively cultivate different levels of responsibility.

Granting your team responsibility doesn’t have to be like switching a faucet on and off, or delegating entire areas at a time. This sounds like common sense, but it’s amazing how many companies do just that — take a team member with little responsibility and abruptly thrust them into the spotlight where all or most of the responsibility for a particular area now falls on them. Pat would argue that responsibility should be like gradually watering a plant, whereas weeks of drought followed by a deluge of water is overwhelming. Sometimes “too much too fast” even sinks team members with the most potential.

In the following lessons:

We'll explore more of the view from the big chair, including:
How to instill responsibility in your team
How to own your area without micromanaging
Responsibility for your personal brand, and why it matters

(Download the transcript below)

Heading

In the video above, listen to neurologist Dr. Roberto Fernandez-Romero talk about Pat and the impact she made in “The Big Chair.”

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 1: Pat's Legacy 
Dr. Roberto Fernandez-Romero 
Although I never had the fortune of meeting Pat personally, unfortunately by the time I joined 
the Pat Summit Clinic as their medical director, she had passed away, I've had the opportunity 
to meet so many people that she deeply touched. And not only that, everything that we do 
every day at our clinic is really inspired by her vision and the strength that she found to come 
out and talk about something so personal and so difficult as her diagnosis. In doing so, she 
really gave a voice to the voiceless and continues every day to make a difference in so many 
people's lives. 
  
So we are very fortunate to have been part of this legacy and to continue on with it in our work 
every day.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 1: Knowing Your Priorities 
Joan Cronan 
You know, in life, it's important that you know your priorities and you live your priorities. If Pat 
Summitt was standing here right now, she would tell you her priorities were academics and 
then athletics. She looked at the basketball court as her classroom. 
  
If you ask her what she was proudest of, she would say, I'm proudest of the academic success 
that every young lady who played for me for four years graduated. She wouldn't say, I won 
eight national championships, I went to 18 final fours. Folks, people dream of going to one final 
four. Pat Summitt went to 18 final fours. Pat Summitt believed in academics.  
 
One of my favorite stories on Pat is when she was recruiting a young lady from Kentucky.  
This young lady was a great athlete, but she came from a very poor part of the world and a very 
poor academic background. And she mentioned to me that she was worried about this young 
lady being able to succeed at Tennessee. Well, in our world, you can go in and visit in their 
home, then you can visit, bring them in and visit on campus. 
  
She went to visit her and she said, Joan, she really wants to come. Of course, as an AD, I said, 
how good is she? And she said, she's really good. So we brought her in to visit on campus. I'll 
never forget that Saturday. It was a Saturday that we had 107,000 people running around in 
Orange. It was a football Saturday. But I went to my office to meet with this young lady. And 
standing there was a tall, attractive, blonde young lady dressed in one of the most expensive 
looking suits that I'd ever seen. You can imagine my mind talk as I visited with her. I was 
picturing poverty and here was this model sitting in front of me. So finally, I said, you know, 
that's one of the prettiest suits I've ever seen. 
  
She gave me the biggest smile. And she said, Ms. Cronin, when Pat came in to visit me, my 
mother drew a picture of the suit that Pat had on. And my mother made this suit for me to 
come visit. 
  
Well, she came and she was successful. I was so excited. And her junior year, she was 
struggling. She was struggling academically. It wasn't that she wasn't trying. It wasn't that she 
wasn't capable. It was kind of like that treadmill you get on. You couldn't catch up. Because I 
called a summit conference.

I called Pat in, I called her academic advisor, and I called the young lady. And we talked about 
what it would take to be successful. And as a team, we decided that we would pull her out of 
practice and pull her off the road for three weeks where she would have time to catch up. 
  
But we'd let her start at every home game. It's that lollipop we gave her to talk about success. 
The academic advisor came back. She said, Joan, she's doing great. So I said, okay. And she 
started competing and she started traveling. 
  
We went down to the SEC tournament, and she made All-Tournament. We lost in the finals, but 
she had made all tournament. I was so glad we hadn't denied her an opportunity to be the best 
she could be. 
  
Fast forward to her senior year, we're playing in the championship game. I'm trying to be sure 
everybody's got their tickets, the alumni are having the reception, the president's plane have 
landed, the coaches have what they need, and my phone rings at the hotel. And I answer it, and 
it's this young lady, and she's crying. 
  
And I said, what's wrong? She said, I wanted you to be the first one to know that UT just called, 
and I made the Dean's List. So she made the Dean's List. She went on to help us win a national 
championship, and she became the first person in her family ever to graduate from college. 
  
That's what I call success. So remember, we are teaching young people to be successful, just 
like you are teaching your employees to be successful and grow.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 2: Responsibility = Accountability = Ownership 
Nicky Anosike 
Responsibility, accountability, ownership. These words are interchangeable, right? Not so 
fast. What if we told you that these three words were a progression that can help you and 
your team get to the next level? 
 
Imagine this. Two customers walk into a busy lobby. There are two frazzled employees 
working the front desk, one answering the phones, the other trying to help another 
customer with some paperwork. As soon as one call ends, the employee picks up the 
phone again to make a follow-up call. The employee helping the previous customer never 
looks up from the computer. They call an employee out of the back to answer a question. 
Neither looks up or acknowledges the growing line of two to three people in front of them. 
When the question is answered, the third employee immediately retreats to the back 
office. After all, he doesn't work in the lobby. The employee on the phone turns her back to 
make it clear that she can't take customers in her line right now. The employee handling 
the customer is growing more and more stressed, cutting the customer off as they try to 
ask what he sees as unnecessary questions. Two additional employees walk in the door for 
their shift, oblivious to the growing line, laughing and joking as they head for the break 
room. Meanwhile, the line grows. 
 
Then the owner of the business walks in. Seeing the growing line of customers, he 
immediately springs into action, paging two additional employees. He then asks 
customers with one set of needs to take the right line, while customers with another set of 
needs to take the left line, smiling and making eye contact with each customer. He quickly 
processes some of the small requests first while asking the others to step aside for more 
detailed service. 
 
When he asked the team members about it later, he gets blank stares. 
• “I had to make some phone calls,” the first employee says. 
• “I was going as fast as I could,” the second employee says. 
• The third employee stares at him blankly. “I don't work the front desk.” 
• The fourth and fifth employees? “We were just getting back from lunch. We weren't 
even on the clock yet, they protest.” 
 
What happened here? A breakdown in teamwork. Yes, customer service, maybe. But Pat 
would say the growing pileup in this circumstance is around the concept of responsibility

versus accountability versus ownership. Everyone might have been responsible for their 
task at hand, but not the overall goal of getting customers in and out with great service. 
 
My freshman year, Pat called me into her office and she said, “Nikki, I know you're used to 
winning a lot of awards, but on this level, you probably won't win those same awards.” And 
she told me that she needed me to be the defensive stopper. So that became my 
responsibility. The game would start, and Pat would put me in the game and say, stop the 
other team's best player. And that was my responsibility. After the game, Pat would tell me 
if I did a good job or if I didn't do such a good job. And sometimes she would actually have 
the other player's statistics to show me how many points I allowed. That was to ensure that 
I would not only be accountable, but that I would take ownership for my performance. And 
the next game, I would do my best to improve. 
 
So how do you exhibit or encourage ownership among your own work team? Let's take a 
look.

Lesson 2 of 8
Taking Responsibility

Heading

As a leader, how many times have you heard or experienced any of the following among your team:

“Don’t look at me — I just answer the phones.”

A team member does what they’re told to do … but if they weren’t told, they wouldn’t really be doing anything.

A team member sends an email that says, “Hi [Name], I don’t do that. Go ask so-and-so.”

A team member executing in an area without being bought-in to the overall result.

Team members sit silently in meetings, without contributing or giving any feedback.

Someone has been at the organization for 10 years but progressed very little career-wise in that time.

What’s wrong with employees these days? You can’t find good ones like you used to, right?
The list above doesn’t have to be the status quo! Assuming you’re hiring good people — or at least reasonably competent people — many times when any of the above takes place, the flaw isn’t with the person, it’s with the expectations and culture of responsibility that have been created at the organization … or lack thereof. The standard for ownership has been set, and the bar is very low.

A sense of ownership is the most powerful weapon a team or organization can have.”

Lesson 3 of 8
Your Employees

Heading

Put yourself in your employee’s shoes for a moment. Has the team been told super-serving is an expectation, for example, or are they simply going “by-the-book?” Are team members rewarded for going the extra mile, or are the consequences and rewards for average service and above-average service basically the same? Are there ways to step into greater levels of responsibility in each role before actually being promoted, or do you have to wait for the title? Are employees encouraged to speak up in a professional way with suggestions for improvement, or rebuked when they say anything?

There’s a famous saying, “You get what you promote.” The reverse can be true as well: “You get what you allow.” If you treat your team members like order-takers or pencil-pushers, that’s generally what you’ll get. If you teach them that they aren’t supposed to think for themselves … they won’t. If you allow mediocre behavior to be the norm, it will become the norm.

On the flip side, if you teach them that they are responsible for the outcome — that their actions have a direct effect on the outcomes of the business and their daily environment — they’re more likely to feel motivated to work hard.
The elusive quality we’re talking about here is ownership.

Exercise

Which of these characterize qualities of ownership vs. no ownership?

(Please click each to complete this element)

No ownership! Owners understand the organization’s priorities and goals.

Ignorance of the business’s priorities

Ownership! Owners have a sense of purpose in their daily routine.

Enthusiasm for their work

No ownership! Owners prioritize quality results.

Lack of attention to detail

Poor customer service

Ownership! Owners focus on improvement and overcome obstacles.

Being solution-oriented

No ownership! All team members are working toward a shared outcome.

Employees vs. leadership mentality

Ownership! Owners understand the big picture and how to get there.

Contributing toward the goal

No ownership! Owners prioritize timeliness and punctuality.

Chronic tardiness

Ownership! Owners are able to put themselves in the customer’s shoes.

Empathy with the customer

No ownership! Ownership often means going above and beyond.

Doing the minimum output

No ownership! Owners understand the need to communicate clearly with other team members.

Poor Communication

Ownership! Owners speak up when they see a problem or opportunity arise.

Giving feedback

Ownership! Owners are always thinking, “What more can I do?” to help the team.

Asking, “What else?”

Lesson 4 of 8
Learning RAO

Learning RAO

People don’t just wake up each day with a sense of ownership. Whether it’s in business or our personal lives, there is a natural progression from responsibility to ownership.
When teaching the Definite Dozen, Pat used the simple formula below:

Responsibility = Accountability = Ownership

When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

It’s in your jurisdiction, and you have both the blessing and ability to control it.

You realize you are answerable for the outcome of the task. “The buck stops with you,” to use the classic phrase. In other words, responsibility is task-oriented, while accountability is outcome-based.

The dictionary defines ownership as “the act, state, or right of possessing something.” It means claiming a particular process, situation, or outcome as your own. Not only are you responsible for it in general, the way a guardian or steward might be, but you actually own it. You are bought-in and fully invested in the outcome or task at hand because it is yours — whether we’re talking about a sports team, a building, or a business. Managers may have responsibility to see that the deck gets polished, but owners are responsible for how the ship looks.

So why is creating a sense of ownership among your team — as much as possible — important? A team full of mini-owners creates an atmosphere of initiative and enthusiasm you can’t cultivate by simply doling out tasks. It’s not as hard to convince someone to keep the house in good shape when they own it.

Heading

And a sense of ownership implies a direct correlation between a team member’s decisions and the outcome of the business. It may not be a direct line — there may be other steps or factors along the way — but there is a connection, and they can start to visualize how their level of performance impacts customer satisfaction or profits.

Not only are you responsible for it in general, the way a guardian or steward might be, but you actually own it. You are bought-in and fully invested in the outcome or task at hand because it is yours — whether we’re talking about a sports team, a building, or a business. Managers may have responsibility to see that the deck gets polished, but owners are responsible for how the ship looks.

body_blocks.text: So why is creating a sense of ownership among your team — as much as possible — important? A team full of mini-owners creates an atmosphere of initiative and enthusiasm you can’t cultivate by simply doling out tasks. It’s not as hard to convince someone to keep the house in good shape when they own it.

items: And a sense of ownership implies a direct correlation between a team member’s decisions and the outcome of the business. It may not be a direct line — there may be other steps or factors along the way — but there is a connection, and they can start to visualize how their level of performance impacts customer satisfaction or profits.

Lesson 6 of 8
Creating a Sense of Ownership

Creating a Sense of Ownership Among Your Team

When it comes to the formula above, Pat knew you couldn’t skip steps.
Commanding people to simply be owners usually doesn’t work. Start where you are — meaning, cultivate responsibility first.
(Scroll through to complete this element)

Summary

In a way, ownership forces team members to think about the big picture — and helps you think about the big picture in a way you may not have been able to before. You have a myriad of owners looking at the goals from a diversity of angles now, in a way that one department manager or leader couldn’t hope to cover alone. You don’t have to preach buy-in; you already have it. All by not being afraid to instill responsibility in your team … and committing to champion them as they step into it.

Does everyone on the team know what they’re responsible for?

Not merely what they’re supposed to be doing or not doing with their time “on the clock,” but do they know what exact areas they’re responsible for?

Is everyone uniquely responsible for something?

This may vary by organization, but take a step back. Do you have six people responsible for steps 1, 2, and 5, for example, but no one responsible for steps 3 and 4? Sometimes articulating responsibility means making some corrections or implementing temporary duties to make sure every person is responsible for something that’s driving toward the bottom line, and no task or area is left without an owner.

Does everyone understand that they are not only responsible, but also accountable for the results of the tasks?

Does the person stocking the grocery bags understand that they aren’t simply putting bags in holsters, but that if the registers run out, they are accountable? Being accountable prompts an entirely new level of thought: How many bags are we going through per day? Do we have enough in the back to last through the week? We went through bags much faster than expected yesterday; should I tell our supply purchaser? Such thoughts are well on their way to ownership.
Does the person responsible for running the social media account understand that they aren’t simply responsible for making posts, but accountable for how those posts are performing — and making the necessary adjustment if the results are subpar? Does the person designing the website know they will be held accountable for the bounce rate — how many customers visit the site and abandon the page without engaging or clicking on anything? Or are they too absorbed with slick graphics and a nice logo? You get the idea.

(Download the transcript below)

Heading

Listen to Corinne Milien, founder and CEO of WRK, recall an ownership lesson under Pat’s mentorship about “rebounding” and always thinking of the next play.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 2: The Next Play 
Corinne Milien 
One time I remember going to the Virgin Islands. Playing in a regular tournament. And just like 
with any tournament, any trip, the expectation is that we're going on an excursion and just 
having a good time. 
Well, on this particular trip, we just happened to lose one game. And the players were not 
having it. The players didn't want to have anything to do with an excursion. They wanted to be 
in their beds and sulk. 
Pat was not letting that happen either. She made sure that those players understood that no 
matter the outcome, you bounce back. You take advantage of the opportunities that you have, 
in this case, being in the Virgin Islands and going on a trip. It's called rebounding. Whatever 
happens, you think of the next play. The next play in this case, again, was going on this trip. 
So anytime I think about, oh man, I don't feel good about doing this, I have to think next play.

Lesson 7 of 8
Knowledge Check

Which of these questions is key to creating a sense of ownership on a team?

Does everyone on the team know what they’re responsible for?

Is everyone uniquely responsible for something?

Does everyone understand that they are not only responsible, but also accountable for the results of the tasks?

All of the above

As Coach Summitt once said, “If you don’t clearly articulate who is responsible for what, _______________.”

When there’s a victory, you won’t know why.

When competing, you won’t know how you match up.

When there’s a breakdown, you won’t know what went wrong.

When there’s obstacles, you won’t know what to do.

What does it mean to have everyone uniquely responsible for something?

You need to establish who is owning each process and detail with minimal overlap.

You need to make sure the entire team is working toward the same thing.

You need to hire a minimum of three people per position.

You won’t get far if everyone is focused on different job duties.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 2: The Power of the T-Shirt Cannon 
Jimmy Delaney 
Over the course of my time with Tennessee Athletics and with women's athletics and with the 
Lady Vols, I was very fortunate to go from being a part of the game atmosphere and doing 
things. Early in my career, I started as the person that dressed up as the mascot and I was the 
person that shot the t-shirt cannon. 
And I remember one game I was in the moment just a little bit too much and I got a little bit too 
close to the team huddle and I shot some t-shirts. And the next day in the office I was called 
into, at that point it was Coach Summit's office. And I sat down and she said, “What happened 
last night?” And I was racking my brain and I couldn't quite remember. 
And she said, “I was coaching in the huddle and I was distracted by the t-shirt cannon. And she 
was like, should I be distracted by that?” And I said, “No, coach, you shouldn't be.” And she 
said, “Look, you go be great at what you're doing and I need to be great at what I'm doing.” And 
she was like, those two things can coexist.

Coach Summit. And we were done. She said, "You got it. And I got it.” And she said, “Great.” 
She said, “But how far can you shoot a t-shirt?” 
And so for me, it was very relieving because where I thought I was about to get grilled and 
toasted and that was the end of my career, she communicated with me. She made her point. 
But then after that, she kind of cleared the air and made it very fun. And I did tell her that I can 
shoot a t-shirt all the way up into the upper deck.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 3: Learning To Macromanage 
Petra Dunn 
Okay, so if we're all acting like owners, some things need to change, right? You need to be 
involved in every detail, every decision. Nothing is too small or too large to escape your notice. 
Be careful, my friend, you are on a slippery slope to micromanagement. Just saying the word 
causes most team members to cringe. 
Did you know there's a way to take ownership without micromanaging? It's called 
macromanaging, and the best leaders learn how to do it well. As a leader, Coach Summit 
realized she couldn't be everywhere. It's impossible. And yet the buck stopped with her for the 
well-being and safety of nearly a dozen young, inexperienced athletes, many of whom were 
only vaguely familiar with discipline and some of whom had never been away from home 
before. It was physically impossible to stand over them at all times. This is where instilling a 
sense of responsibility and ownership in your team and knowing when to back off comes in 
handy. 
You may not be leading athletes like Pat. You're leading employees, but the same principle still 
applies. If you rush into every situation to help dot every I, cross every T, and help get the ox 
out of the ditch, will employees learn the buck stops with them or with you? 
So, what are some examples of micromanaging versus macromanaging?  
 
Micromanaging might look something like: 
• Approving every email before it is sent. 
• Frequently redoing employees' work instead of providing feedback. 
• Dictating the exact method for completing a task or giving overly detailed instructions 
for simple tasks. 
• Requiring excessive approval for small expenses. 
• Requiring employees to track their daily activities in minute detail. 
• You know the signs. Likely you've seen this before.  
 
By contrast, macromanaging might look something like:  
• Setting clear overall goals and letting employees determine the best way to achieve 
them. 
• Holding periodic check-ins rather than constant monitoring.

• Encouraging autonomy and decision-making for projects someone is owning 
• Evaluating employees based on results and outcomes, not time spent on an activity or 
doing an activity a certain way. 
Take a minute to stop and think where you fall on the scale of micromanagement versus 
macromanagement. 
So how do you take the mantle of authority as a leader while also empowering your team to be 
mini-owners and experts in their craft? We'll take a closer look in this lesson.

Lesson 2 of 7
Knowing the Signs

Heading

The truth is, some leaders — well-meaning leaders — get this far into understanding responsibility and ownership and then get stuck. Their extreme sense of responsibility spills over into the dreaded world of micromanaging.
Click on each circle in the illustration below for examples of micromanaging.

Being in every meeting

Approving every marketing asset

Being copied on every email

Weighing in on every problem

Making every decision

Sitting in on every new hire interview

Approving every purchase

Maybe this rings a bell with you or someone you know. After all, that’s unconditional ownership, right?
Not necessarily.

If you have a company of 10 people total, maybe some of these responsibilities do fall on you. Chances are, though, you’re not in that category. Or maybe you started in that category and grew out of it long ago, but you’re still operating like you’re a one-person band.

And know what’s worse? It starts to crush those you lead. With your fingers in every pie, the team never learns how to cook, metaphorically speaking. People either gravitate toward two areas: They don’t think for themselves (why would they, if you’re going to wind up making every decision for the group?) or they’re so terrified to make a mistake they can’t do anything without approval. They default to order-takers, and any unique characteristics or skills you hired them for in the first place get buried.

If your time had a dollar amount of what you’re worth to the company (not your literal hourly wage, but the amount of money your decisions bring in per month), would the best use of your time be researching costs for a new type of coffee in the break room or rewriting the second paragraph of the company newsletter? What about sitting in four meetings each week about processes and procedures? Deciding whether a button on a website will be green or blue? What picture should go in the new brochure?Probably none of the above. There are certain things that only you can do, and it’s most important to make time for those.

Exercise

Which of these is an unintended outcome of micromanaging?
Drag and drop each card to complete this element.

It takes your time away from other more important duties.

Your team learns to do things on their own.

It starts to crush those you lead.

It’s unscalable.

Your team won’t learn to think for themselves.

Your team will be terrified to make mistakes.

The team becomes order-takers.

The team will be hesitant to do anything without approval.

Your teammates learn when to consult you and when to take risks.

Team members like it.

You will have more free time in your day.

Outcome of Micromanaging

Outcome of Macromanaging

Lesson 3 of 7
Manage Things, Lead People

Heading

When leaders realize that wearing themselves out over details like the above is not only making them tired, but squashing their team, it can be a freeing revelation.
So, how do you hold yourself responsible for all the things that can go right or wrong without being involved in the day-to-day operations?
Part of it goes back to the classic definition of leadership. You may have heard it before:
You manage things, and you lead people.

The people as a team do the thing, whether it’s running a company or winning a national championship, and you lead them to do it well, like Pat did. Their achievement is your achievement, the team’s achievement, so you train them to do it well. Then get out of the way.

That’s it. That doesn’t mean you don’t step in in an emergency. That doesn’t mean you’re always in the dark. You don’t do it for them, you don’t do it with them. You hire smart people, people who are a good fit, and make sure they have what they need to do their job well.

Lesson 4 of 7
Being Hands Off

What Does It Take to Be "Hands-Off"?

Understanding the importance of being “hands off” is one of the most fundamental (and often overlooked) tenets of good leadership.

Sometimes as a leader, we think our strength lies in getting the team to produce a certain level of output — after all, it’s what we’re all responsible for. You may even be tempted to jump in and help them. But at the end of the day, you can’t make people do things. You have to lead them. All you can really do is hire well.

We’ll say it again. All you can really do is get the right people in the right seat on the bus and lead them well to do their jobs. You can’t force them to do it with excellence, innovation, positivity, super-service, or creativity. All you can do is fire them if they don’t and replace them with someone else who will. Then the cycle starts again.

Heading

As the leader, you have to lead them in attitude, vision, excellence, motivation — all the principles Pat championed in the Definite Dozen — guiding them to the level of self-discipline, autonomy, or ingenuity you want.
They will know what that level is because it will be modeled by you. Not done by you on behalf of the team or for the team but encouraged by the level of leadership you provide.

Exercise

Which of these is an example of being “hands-off” vs “hands-on”?
Drag and drop each card to complete this element.

Letting team members experiment with new methods

Daily status meetings

Focusing on results, not minute-by-minute activity

Not needing to approve every small decision

Overseeing each step of a project

Excessive reporting

Encouraging problem-solving

Dictating how to do things

Hands-off

Hands-on

Lesson 5 of 7
Micromanaging vs. Macromanaging

(Download the transcript below)

Heading

Listen to Sr. Vice President Petra Dunn of Merrill Lynch Wealth Management remember how she learned to delegate and become more “hands off” in her early career.

Exercise

Which of the following is an example of micromanaging vs. macromanaging?
Drag and drop each card to complete this element.

Approving minor updates to the website

Asking for a monthly update report from your team

Showing the writing team how to write articles

Picking out the wine options for an incentive lunch

Having your employees keep an hourly log

Approving major product initiatives

Making sure the team knows that without you, they'd be lost

Stepping in to take over a project when a team member stumbles

Leading a quarterly meeting for your team

Being copied on the test send of every outgoing email

Outlining the one-, five-, and 10-year vision for your area

Making sure all ideas for the product come from you

Having an open-door policy

Hosting an offsite retreat for your team members

Making a note of the time the admin spends away from their desk

Overtaking the new-hire training to make sure it’s done "right"

Asking the finance team to cc you on every invoice, no matter how small

Having one-on-ones with team members you manage

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 3: Delegating 
Petra Dunn 
One of the most transformational moments in my early career was when I was given my first 
independent assignment after completing a management training program. I got called up to 
the executive vice president's office and he said, “Petra, we have an assignment we'd like to 
offer you. We have a branch that has been losing money for well over a year. The branch 
manager passed away and we've seen a lot of client attrition, but we think you could develop 
strong relationships and turn it around. I won't sugarcoat this. It's going to be tough. And if 
you're not able to turn it around, no one will look negatively on you. However, if you succeed, it 
will be an opportunity for you to shine.” 
I had it turned around in six months, and it felt great. 
I remember when I brought my partner on about 10 years ago. She had a great resume, good 
character, and a strong work ethic, but no experience in my industry. However, I knew I could 
teach her those skills. In our business, mistakes can be very costly, so it was no surprise that she 
wanted to run every decision by me. Soon, I realized I needed to teach her to take 
accountability for making her own decisions, but I also realized I would have to train her to 
carefully assess risk and have the confidence to own her own decisions. 
I told her that as long as she followed the process I had taught her, I would always have her 
back, even if she made a mistake. She developed into a great advisor and a wonderful business 
partner.

Lesson 1 of 10
Personal Brand: What’s Yours?

(Download the transcript below)

Heading

One last part of responsibility, and one that often gets overlooked, is the responsibility for personal brand. You’ve likely heard the term “personal brand” over the years, whether you’ve given much thought to yours or not.
A personal brand is a unique identity that defines who you are, what you stand for, and how you are perceived by others. It encompasses your personality, values, skills, achievements, and reputation. In today's world, personal branding has become an important aspect of one's professional success. A strong personal brand can help you establish a professional image, increase your credibility, and stand out from the competition.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 4: Personal Brand: What’s Yours? 
Morgan Vance 
The King, The Iron Lady, The People's Princess, The Notorious B.I.G., The Baltimore Bullet, The 
Queen of Country Music. Chances are, each of these statements brought a unique individual to 
mind, and these names were given for a reason: Elvis Presley, Margaret Thatcher, Princess 
Diana, Christopher Wallace, Michael Phelps, and Dolly Parton. 
These people were each known for a certain set of attributes, including having a very, very 
strong personal brand. You may not be a celebrity, pop star, or talk show host, but you yourself 
do have a personal brand. We all do. And while we can't control a lot of the things that go on 
around us, no one can control your personal brand but you. You are responsible for the 
attitude, image, and skill set that comes to mind when people think of you. 
Have you ever thought about it before? Maybe, maybe not, but it's real, whether we choose to 
think about it or not. So what do you want people to think about when your name comes to 
mind? What do they currently think of? 
When I was growing up, I knew I wanted to be a leader and make a difference in my 
community, but I also knew I wanted to be a mom. Growing up in Knoxville, I received the 
benefit of watching strong female leaders like Pat build their personal brands. She was a leader 
both on and off the court and showed me that you could be successful in both your 
professional and personal life. 
I will never forget watching her come to high school basketball games and sit silently on the 
front row, rooting on her son. She didn't draw attention to herself. She didn't let her 
professional work come into her personal time. She was there to be a mom. 
The truth is, personal brand matters and you can shape yours. Let's start by defining what a 
personal brand is. Your personal brand is a unique combination of your skills, experiences, 
values, and personality that sets you apart from others. It's your identity, how you present 
yourself to the world, both online and offline. 
Whether it's through your interactions with colleagues, social media, or the skills you provide as 
part of your daily routine, your personal brand is always on display. Personal brand is the key to 
differentiating yourself from others with similar skills or qualifications. By showcasing your 
unique strengths, passions, and values, you position yourself as a distinct and memorable 
individual. 
An authentic personal brand is one that aligns with your true self. Trying to be someone you're 
not can be exhausting and unsustainable in the long run. At its core, a positive personal brand is

built on attitude and trustworthiness. When you consistently deliver on your promises and 
showcase your expertise, you establish credibility in your field. 
A strong personal brand can leave a lasting positive impression, opening doors to new 
opportunities. So take a minute and think about where you are with your personal brand. What 
things do you like? What don't you like? And this lesson will explore the concept of personal 
brands some more, as well as exercises you can do to uncover yours.

Lesson 3 of 10
Responsibility for Personal Brand

Heading

How many times have you heard these words:
(Click on each circle in the illustration below to complete this element)

“I don’t care what people think of me.”

“If they don’t like me, that’s their fault.”

“Why should I change how I communicate?”

“I’m not here to make friends.”

“I’m just here to get a job done, not make small talk.”

You may have even thought some of these yourself! These statements revolve around the concept of personal brand, and the speaker’s willingness (or lack thereof) to change anything about their brand.
You may be tempted to dismiss personal brand, say that it doesn’t matter, or even put the responsibility on others, thinking it’s their job to have a good opinion about you. But the truth is, personal brand is a unique area of responsibility — no one can be responsible for your personal brand but you.

Exercise

Drag and drop each card to complete this element.

“I want to be the best version of myself.”

“That’s just the way I am. They don’t have to like it.”

“Why does it matter how I dress?”

“I care about my appearance.”

“What are some things I can improve on?”

“How I communicate shouldn’t matter.”

Lack of awareness

Aware

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 4 of 10
The Queen of Rocky Top

Heading

The Legend. The General. The Queen of Rocky Top. The Torchbearer. The Godmother of Women’s Basketball.
Pat herself had a strong personal brand built around her dedication to the sport, her unwavering work ethic, and commitment to excellence both on and off the court. She was known for her toughness, her ability to motivate and inspire her players, and her strong leadership skills. She was also known for her composure, the “Summitt Stare,” and her well-manicured look on the sidelines.

Believe it or not, Pat’s own personal brand went through quite a transformation in a period of just a few short years. Raised on a farm in Henrietta, Tenn., in high school she was known as Trish (short for Patricia) Head. When she went to college, her sorority friends assumed she was Pat, and she didn’t correct them.
“Trish Head was a farm kid with crooked teeth and all the wrong clothes who said ain’t, reckon, and yonder,” Pat recalled. “You never get a second chance to make a first impression. In those early days at college, I realized that presentation counts. For better or worse, strangers made sweeping judgements based on my appearance and demeanor. So, I began the process of self-transformation.”1

She quickly enlisted two friends to help her with her grammar and accent, and she enrolled in speech classes. “I began to pay attention to my clothes,” she said. “Dressing appropriately for a role can help you play it better.” She began to wear tailored suits on the sidelines and got braces when she was nearly 30.
In a few short years, gone was the shy farm kid who always wore jeans and was self-conscious about her height. Summitt’s players affectionately referred to her as “Sarge” for her command and polish on the sidelines. Pat herself had a strong personal brand built around her dedication to the sport, her unwavering work ethic, and commitment to excellence both on and off the court. body_blocks.text:
Believe it or not, Pat’s own personal brand went through quite a transformation in a period of just a few short years. Raised on a farm in Henrietta, Tenn., in high school she was known as Trish (short for Patricia) Head. When she went to college, her sorority friends assumed she was Pat, and she didn’t correct them.
“Trish Head was a farm kid with crooked teeth and all the wrong clothes who said ain’t, reckon, and yonder,” Pat recalled. “You never get a second chance to make a first impression. In those early days at college, I realized that presentation counts. For better or worse, strangers made sweeping judgements based on my appearance and demeanor. So, I began the process of self-transformation.”1

She quickly enlisted two friends to help her with her grammar and accent, and she enrolled in speech classes. “I began to pay attention to my clothes,” she said. “Dressing appropriately for a role can help you play it better.” She began to wear tailored suits on the sidelines and got braces when she was nearly 30.

Summitt’s players affectionately referred to her as “Sarge” for her command and polish on the sidelines. Others called her “The Iron Lady” and marveled at her ability to consistently appear in a polished wardrobe reflecting the University of Tennessee’s signature colors. She even became known for a particular shade of blue: “Summitt Blue,” now recognized and worn by the University of Tennessee in athletic uniforms.

Lesson 5 of 10
Why Personal Brand Is Important

Heading

As someone who spent their life in the spotlight, Summitt’s personal brand was well-known. Your own brand may be less distinct, but it exists all the same. We’ll say it again: Your personal brand exists, whether you recognize that it does or not!

Scroll through to complete this element.

What Is Personal Brand?

Personal brand incorporates a lot of things, but without overcomplicating it, there are four main parts:
●      Attitude
●      Image
●      Skills
●      Experience

Conclusion

When considering what your personal brand is, consider what you are known for specifically in each of these four main areas.

Attitude

What is the attitude you present in your role? What principles do you stand for? How do you communicate?

Image

What words would others use to describe you? What is your own signature look? What are you known for?

Skills

What expertise can you be counted on for? What things do you bring to the table? What is your superpower or special skill in your role?

Experience

Finally, what experiences make you unique? What events in your background are you known for that make up part of who you are?

Lesson 7 of 10
Does it Matter?

Does Personal Brand Matter if the Output Is Good?

You may ask, “Does personal brand at work really matter if my output is good?” In a word, yes. In fact, it matters a whole lot more than you may think.

Personal brand affects consideration for promotions, specific tasks you’re given, what information you can be trusted with, whether you’re asked to present in a meeting, and whether your teammates want to work with you and follow you. After all, no one wants to work with (or follow) a successful jerk.

Your personal brand can have a profound impact on your personal life too, including your relationships and your overall success. Personal brand can sometimes even make up for a direct lack of skill or experience in certain areas.

Lesson 8 of 10
What Is Your Brand?

Heading

The first step is realizing what your personal brand is currently. In the exercises at the end of this lesson, we’ll go over a few tips for uncovering what your brand may be at the moment, and how you are perceived by others.

What Is Your Personal Brand?

The next step is evaluating what you would like your personal brand to be.
(Scroll through to complete this element)

Summary

Changing your personal brand takes time and effort. It may take weeks or months to see the results you want, but if you stay focused and committed, like Coach Summitt, you will eventually shape a winning, successful brand.

Identify your goals

What do you want to achieve with your personal brand? Do you want to be known for a particular skill or quality?

Develop a plan

Is there a gap between the image you’re projecting and the brand you would like to have?

Seek out opportunities

Look for opportunities to showcase your personal brand.

Personal Reflections

When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 4: Getting a Speeding Ticket with Pat 
Jimmy Delaney 
Pat notoriously was late. She would never tell you this, but she was always late. And she was 
always running behind and always kind of doing makeup in the car and all of that. 
And so anytime that was happening, if I was with her, I would always say, "Let me drive and you 
go in the passenger seat." And we were late. And she told me to get there as quick as I could 
because she didn't want to be late and didn't want that kind of image on her or whatever it 
was. 
And so, we were driving and I was going well above the speed limit. And next thing I know, the 
red and blue lights are behind us. And I was like, "Pat, we're getting pulled over." And she's like, 
"All right, we'll pull over." 
And so, we pull over and I knew I was doing almost double the speed limit. And I was like, "This 
is going to be really, really bad." And I'm starting to dig out my ID and all of this kind of stuff. 
And the officer was walking up with a very angry look on his face because he was pulling over a 
very nice car that was going way too fast. 
And I rolled down the window and before I could say a word, Pat from the passenger seat leans 
over against me and almost kind of like pushes me back into the seat. She's like, "Officer, I'm 
sorry. It's all my fault. I'm late. And I just, you know, we were trying to get there as quick as we 
could." 
And the officer never made eye contact with me, straight to Pat. And he's like, "Now coach, you 
know you're not supposed to be driving that fast," as if I was like a ghost driving the car or 
whatever it was. 
She was like, "I know, I'm so sorry. We're just trying to get to West Knoxville for this thing. I 
promise I won't do it again." 
And he's like, "All right, coach. Good to see you. Good luck this season." 
And so, I'm sitting there like, "What in the world just happened here?" And I roll the window 
back up and I look at her, and she goes back and she goes, "Hit it." And we just took off.

items.paragraph: Pat’s own personal brand was larger than life. Listen to UT Associate Athletics Director Jimmy Delaney tell the story of getting a speeding ticket with Coach Summitt on the way to an athletic event.

items.heading: Personal Reflections
items.paragraph: Refer to your workbook for the reflection questions and exercises below.
What do you think your personal brand is currently?
What would you like your personal brand to be?
Who has a personal brand you admire? Why?
Who around you has a negative personal brand? What are some of the characteristics?
In your opinion, what is the hardest part about developing a personal brand?

items.heading: Exercises
items.paragraph: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.
What three words do you want others to think of you when they hear your name?

Create your own personal brand statement. Use the sample statement to get started or come up with your own.

“I am a _____ who does ______ and is known for _______, ________, and _________.”
What nontechnical attributes do you envision going along with your personal brand (dress, overall presence, key relationships, work ethic, etc.)?
Where do you need to close the gap in some of these areas?
Audit your personal brand online and outside of work. How do you represent yourself on your social media profiles? What may need to change? What may need to be added?
What are the next action steps you can take to enhance your personal brand this month?

Sources:

  1. Unless otherwise noted, all quotes taken from, Reach for the Summitt, by Pat Summitt and Sally Jenkins. Three Rivers Press. 1998.

Lesson 1 of 9
Communicating to Win

(Download the transcript below)

Heading

Good communication is a key part of any successful workplace team. Clear communication helps foster positive relationships between colleagues, improves productivity, and ultimately, leads to better outcomes for your organization. It’s no wonder Pat’s fourth Definite Dozen principle was Learn to be a Great Communicator.
And yet, it’s worth a closer look, because even though communication is the glue that holds a team together, many organizations fail to grasp just how essential it is to prioritize good communication over other principles like processes, speed, authority, or confidentiality.
As Pat would say, the first step is not merely viewing communication as a component of a healthy team. It’s realizing that communication is everything.

You can have the brightest, most creative people in the world, but if they can’t communicate, you won’t fully comprehend what they’re capable of.”

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 5: Communicating to Win 
Jimmy Delaney 
Few people would disagree. Communication is the cornerstone of success, whether you're in 
personal or professional settings. It's the lifeblood of any high-functioning team and a core 
principle in Pat's famous Definite Dozen leadership principles. Communication is more than just 
words. It's the bridge that connects team members. Clear and open communication builds 
trust, respect, and cooperation, whether it's face-to-face, virtual meetings, or written 
messages. Miscommunication can have severe consequences. When we fail to express 
ourselves clearly, it can lead to confusion, conflict, and missed opportunities. 
Here at Tennessee, communication is key to everything that we do for a successful event, 
whether we're having 50 people for a private event or 100,000 people for a football game. 
Communication ultimately is what drives our success. 
Earlier in my career, I realized how vital communication was. I was trying to do many things on 
my own, and I realized that teamwork and communication was going to bring all of our ideas 
together. By not communicating the entire plan to the entire team that was helping us, 
ultimately, I ended up taking more of the work on myself, dropping some of those balls, and 
ultimately it wasn't as successful as it was. In that, I learned to communicate with everybody, 
even somebody that may not be helping you or could have an opportunity to help you, still 
communicate with them because you never know where you might need them for us on a 
game day. 
To give another example, let's say John was preparing for an important client presentation but 
only mentioned it casually to a few colleagues in passing. He didn't really provide any context or 
seek their input formally. Then the day before the presentation, he realized he needed more 
information and hastily sent out a request for feedback. However, most team members were 
unprepared to provide useful input on such a short notice. They didn't have enough context on 
what he was asking to be able to help out in a meaningful way. 
Or let's say his colleague Marcy had a major project she was working on and sent a brief, vague 
email to the team, assuming they would understand their roles and responsibilities. And the 
email lacked supporting details, such as the why or the overall goal of the project. Marcy 
entered all of the tasks into the project management system but never followed up to make 
sure everyone had received them or understood the instructions in the tasks. What kind of 
results do you think she got? You guessed it. The cost of miscommunication or under-
communication can be high. You may have even experienced some of these outcomes yourself.

By contrast, over-communicating, especially when in doubt, is a powerful strategy to prevent 
miscommunication and bridge gaps in understanding. So is providing context. You may already 
be working several methods of this into your weekly rhythms, and that's great. Most teams use 
a variety of the following to make sure communication is running smoothly and flowing freely 
among the team: 
Daily stand-ups: brief, focused meetings where the team shares progress, upcoming tasks, and 
any obstacles they are facing. This keeps everyone aligned and aware of each other's activities, 
allowing for quick problem-solving. 
Regular feedback loops: regularly scheduled one-on-one meetings between team members and 
their managers provide a platform for constructive feedback. 
Quick-time communication tools: using tools like Microsoft Teams, Slack, or Trello for ongoing 
communication and project management ensures that all team members can collaborate 
effectively, regardless of their location. Here at Tennessee, we use both Slack and Trello, and 
because we are all over the place and working on many different things, not worried about 
which email is the most recent, Slack, a real-time communication tool, helps us out 
tremendously. 
Taking the time to communicate well at its core is a powerful mark of respect. Let's take a 
minute to learn more.

Lesson 3 of 9
When in Doubt, Overcommunicate

Learning to Overcommunicate

The heart of communicating to win can be summed up in four words: When in doubt, overcommunicate.
For best results, always err on the side of overcommunicating, rather than under-communicating. What does this look like?
It means that it’s better to communicate too much than too little, particularly when there’s ambiguity around a task or project. Overcommunicating means providing more information or updates than might be strictly necessary. When you overcommunicate, you ensure that everyone involved in a project or task has all the information they need to do their jobs effectively. This can help to prevent misunderstandings, delays, and mistakes.
Let’s take a look at two sample scenarios:

Scenario 1

To give a practical example, let’s say the vice president is asking for everyone’s weekly report or status updates, including a monthly revenue update, by Thursday morning instead of Monday morning, and you’re in charge of getting it from the team members you manage. You announce this in the next daily standup — revenue updates and estimates from their department are now due on Thursday. What’s to be misunderstood; it’s super clear, right?
For starters, three team members aren’t in the standup. One walked in late, and a few people were having a separate conversation in the back of the room about something urgent. Thursday morning rolls around and … you guessed it, you’re short five reports (including one person who “just forgot”). A few others turned in the weekly status update as usual but included the monthly revenue update as month-to-date instead of projected estimates for the end of the month like you asked. You think, This is unbelievable. People can’t follow simple instructions.
You now have to scramble to give the vice president the numbers she needs, furiously emailing the team members who have missing reports, demanding they send you something ASAP. The truth is, in the words of Cool Hand Luke, “What we have here, is a failure to communicate.”
With just an ounce of prevention — or rather, overcommunication — you might have had a different outcome.

Scenario 2

Let’s say you make the announcement in standup, followed by an email to everyone afterward reinforcing the announcement that you need reports by Thursday, including a brief, bulleted list of what needs to be in the report. Then, Wednesday you send a reminder, including a sample report attached to the email, asking those who can’t send you the report by Thursday morning to let you know in advance. Thursday rolls around, and this time you have all your reports, except for a team member who is at a funeral and communicated that in advance. Or if still you don’t have all your reports for some reason, it becomes easier to address the failure directly with the individuals involved, now that the excuse of communication is taken out of the loop.

Heading

These two examples show how the smallest things can make a difference in the area of communication at work.

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 4 of 9
An Ounce of Prevention

Heading

Overcommunicating can also help you avoid a lot of unnecessary drama on the team.

To give another example, let’s say you have to fire a salesperson who wasn’t getting the job done. When this was mentioned, the team member didn’t react kindly to the criticism and went off on an inappropriate tirade listing all the faults of your organization. You terminate them, but to help the employee save face, you decide to omit the details, sending a cryptic “Steve is no longer with our organization” email. After all, this is confidential, and it’s no one else’s business, right? You decide to follow up verbally with more details two days later in a staff meeting.

The trouble is, Steve was well-liked among the team. Several are good friends with Steve outside of work. The people reporting to Steve who find out in the email at the same time as everyone else are now shocked, confused, and worried about what will happen next. They received all their training from Steve. Did he do something wrong? Rumors are flying by lunchtime as to who will be taking Steve’s place. One person heard it was because Steve questioned the new learning management system’s efficacy and warns people it’s “not safe to speak up anymore with feedback.” A few people text Steve directly, who, still wounded, says the company “has had it out for him all along.” By 3 p.m., half the team is upset that the organization could do such a thing to poor Steve.

Sound familiar? The details may vary, but you may have experienced some version of this at your organization because information was scant and the details were fuzzy. People were left to fill in the gaps of what actually happened with the limited knowledge they had. Overcommunicating doesn’t mean violating someone’s privacy, but with a bit more communication, a lot of the drama above could have been avoided.

A Better Way

To overcommunicate might look something like this: The people who report to or are closest to Steve are told first and given the most information. Without getting into details about Steve’s performance or feelings about the company, they are told whether Steve left on good terms or bad and whether reaching out to Steve might be sensitive at the moment. They are told whether it was one-sided or mutual, and that Steve expressed discontent with his current situation and role. Then, an email goes out to the whole team letting them know of Steve’s departure, that Christine will be temporarily overseeing his area in the interim, and to please direct any questions about his departure or projects to Andrew. They are told that Steve was part of the discussion about leaving and expressed discontent in his area, but the company is grateful for his service and wishes him the very best in his next chapter.

Exercise

Which of these is an example of overcommunicating vs under-communicating? Sort the cards into their correct category.
Drag and drop each card to complete this element.

Having a project kickoff meeting with all parties involved

Sending important information in a one-time email

Only communicating on a need-to-know basis

Making an announcement in a meeting with team members missing

Sending a meeting recap

Following a verbal announcement with an email

An intranet notice for employees to discover on their own

Posting important principles or core values in a prominent location

Overcommunicating

Under-communicating

You terminate them, but to help the employee save face, you decide to omit the details, sending a cryptic “Steve is no longer with our organization” email. After all, this is confidential, and it’s no one else’s business, right? You decide to follow up verbally with more details two days later in a staff meeting.

The trouble is, Steve was well-liked among the team. Several are good friends with Steve outside of work. The people reporting to Steve who find out in the email at the same time as everyone else are now shocked, confused, and worried about what will happen next. They received all their training from Steve. Did he do something wrong? Rumors are flying by lunchtime as to who will be taking Steve’s place. One person heard it was because Steve questioned the new learning management system’s efficacy and warns people it’s “not safe to speak up anymore with feedback.” A few people text Steve directly, who, still wounded, says the company “has had it out for him all along.” By 3 p.m., half the team is upset that the organization could do such a thing to poor Steve.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Sound familiar? The details may vary, but you may have experienced some version of this at your organization because information was scant and the details were fuzzy. People were left to fill in the gaps of what actually happened with the limited knowledge they had. Overcommunicating doesn’t mean violating someone’s privacy, but with a bit more communication, a lot of the drama above could have been avoided.

To overcommunicate might look something like this: The people who report to or are closest to Steve are told first and given the most information. Without getting into details about Steve’s performance or feelings about the company, they are told whether Steve left on good terms or bad and whether reaching out to Steve might be sensitive at the moment. They are told whether it was one-sided or mutual, and that Steve expressed discontent with his current situation and role. Then, an email goes out to the whole team letting them know of Steve’s departure, that Christine will be temporarily overseeing his area in the interim, and to please direct any questions about his departure or projects to Andrew. They are told that Steve was part of the discussion about leaving and expressed discontent in his area, but the company is grateful for his service and wishes him the very best in his next chapter.

Which of these is an example of overcommunicating vs under-communicating? Sort the cards into their correct category.

Drag and drop each card to complete this element.

Sending important information in a one-time email
Only communicating on a need-to-know basis
Making an announcement in a meeting with team members missing
Sending a meeting recap
Following a verbal announcement with an email
An intranet notice for employees to discover on their own
Posting important principles or core values in a prominent location
