Lesson 5: Communicating Eliminates Confusion 
Alexis Hornbuckle 
Powerful conversations include communication. Coach used to always say, communication 
eliminates confusion. And that wasn't just on defense. It wasn't just in the film room. It was in 
life. 
I remember, guys, I got stories for days. I remember in a game, I had broken my wrist, came 
back to play, wrist still broken. And as a guard, my leadership was still important. So, she told 
me, it doesn't matter that you have one hand or that you can't go to your right the way that 
you want. You still need to set up the play. And you need to talk to your teammates about how 
to get to where you want them to get to help you. 
Coach, I'm trying. Communication eliminates confusion as she stares through my soul with 
those icy blue eyes. And I knew instantly all I had to do was open up my mouth, talk, direct, and 
be a leader. Communication can solve a whole lot of problems.

Lesson 7 of 9
Provide Context

Heading

A wise person once said, “You get better results with a little of the why.” Inexperienced leaders tend to default to keeping people in the dark, but experienced leaders know team member buy-in is crucial for a healthy, functioning team. Pat made it clear on her teams that every task or mandate was working toward a particular goal — from the overall goal of national championships to the micro-goals of slowing down a star shooter on the other team or adjusting the defense strategy for an upcoming team who was more physical than they were.

“Because I said so” is usually easier than slowing down to explain the strategy or exact reason behind the ask, but remember: Your success rises and falls on the shoulders of your team. If they can do a better job with more context than less, this ought to be the standard.

For example, you could tell your social media coordinator to spotlight a certain product more, and they may add two or three more posts to the monthly calendar. But if you let them know the why — that this product is eventually going to become the foundation for replacing two other products and that sales need to exceed a certain point — you’re likely to get better results. What’s more, your team may surprise you by thinking of additional ways to reach the goal that you hadn’t considered.

Exercise

Which of these is an example of providing context?
Please click each to complete this element.

Yes! This demonstrates respect.

Letting team members know the reason behind an ask

Yes! This encourages understanding and buy-in.

Explaining the goals for your department

No, consensus is not needed when providing context.

Make sure everyone agrees with the decision

Yes! This sets them up for success.

Giving team members the tools they need to accomplish a task

No, this may lead to confusion.

Adding tasks in the project management system without explanation

No, this encourages confusion.

Keeping strategic direction a secret

Lesson 8 of 9
Set People Up to Win

Heading

Communicating frequently, with context, usually gives team members most of the information they need to win, paired with the practice of setting proper expectations. Don’t leave an abundance of dots for the team to connect on their own. When it comes to setting expectations: To be unclear is to be unkind. No one wants to charge the lane and realize that what they thought was the target wasn’t the target or the way they were expending all their time and energy wasn’t really what the organization wanted. Set your team members up to win.
When individuals win, the team wins. And when the team wins, your organization wins.

Exercise

Which of these is an example of setting people up to win? Sort the cards below into the correct categories.
Drag and drop each card to complete this element.

Introducing them to team members they’ll be working with closely

Communicating complex assignments via email

Having team members with overlapping job duties

Outlining department goals and objectives

Understaffing to save money

Explaining personal key results areas

Creating unnecessary competition

Having periodic check-ins

Outlining clearly who is responsible for what

Ensuring the team has the proper resources to do their work

Setting People Up to Win

NOT Setting People Up to Win

Personal Reflections

How much context do you provide for your team in your current communication? Is it easy or hard to give context?

When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

Lesson 1 of 8
Fairways and Forest Fires

(Download the transcript below)

Heading

Now that we understand the importance of overcommunicating, the next step is understanding how to effectively communicate.
“By communicate effectively, what I mean is, how can you best command the attention of those you are speaking to?” Pat once said. “Should you employ high decibels or low? Are you talking to your boss or your employee? Would a touch of humor help? Decide what you are trying to accomplish, whether you are trying to motivate, elicit a confession, ask for a raise, or instill confidence. Be clear on what you want to say, and say it in a way that is appropriate to your surroundings. Circumstances dictate how you need to speak. You don't holler at a golf tournament. And you don't whisper at a forest fire.”

Pat believed there are three key components to effective personal communication:

Tone

Situation

Nonverbal Communication

We’ll discuss all three a little more in the next lesson.

I wouldn’t speak to a player in my office the same way I would on the court. Circumstances dictate how you need to speak, or whether you need to just shut up and listen. You don’t holler at a golf tournament. You don’t whisper in a forest fire.”

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 6: Fairways and Forest Fires 
Michelle Marciniak 
We've all heard it said before, it's not just about what you say, but also how you say it. This is 
just as true in the workplace as it is anywhere else. Understanding the importance of situational 
and nonverbal communication can make a significant difference in developing a positive and 
productive team. And it all starts with you as the leader. 
Before we dive into the nitty-gritty, let's take a moment to understand the power of tone in 
communication. Tone refers to the emotional quality behind the words we use, whether in 
spoken or written form. It conveys our attitudes, emotions, and intentions impacting how our 
messages are received by others. 
Suppose you came up to a colleague after a presentation where they dropped their coffee on 
their notes. That didn't go well, you joke, smiling. Suppose you came up to the same colleague 
afterwards with a stern look on your face. That didn't go well, you announce in a serious, 
somewhat ominous tone. 
In the workplace, context matters. We need to be mindful of the situations we find ourselves in 
and tailor our communication accordingly. Take a team meeting, for instance. An overly 
aggressive tone might shut down ideas and squash your team's feedback. On the other hand, if 
a team member has been making inappropriate comments or getting out of hand, a firm tone 
may be entirely appropriate. 
In a one-on-one with your team members especially, it's essential to strike a balance between 
being supportive and providing constructive feedback. A dismissive tone can make the 
employee feel unimportant, while a caring and constructive tone can inspire growth. Feedback 
given in a harsh tone can be taken much differently than feedback in a positive tone. 
In general, there are four quadrants of vocal variety: 
Loud and slow conveys authority. You might use this when addressing an issue that is critical 
and there needs to be no room for misunderstanding. 
Loud and fast communicates enthusiasm. You might use this when you are introducing a new 
idea in a meeting and you need to generate excitement. 
Low and slow communicates sincerity and empathy. This tone you might use when you're 
consoling a team member or delivering difficult news. 
Soft and fast conveys anticipation. You might use this tone to communicate upcoming changes, 
almost as if you are letting someone in on a secret.

Knowing how and when to use different tones appropriately can be the difference between 
coming off as authoritative or weak, sensitive or insensitive, excited or unenthusiastic. 
Remember, our words are just one part of the message we convey. Research suggests that up 
to 93% of communication is nonverbal. That means that our body language, facial expressions, 
and tone of voice play a big part in how our messages are interpreted. 
So, how can we be a part of creating a positive communication culture in the workplace? Self-
awareness is the first step in becoming effective communicators. With that in mind, let's dive 
in.

Now that we understand the importance of overcommunicating, the next step is understanding how to effectively communicate.

“By communicate effectively, what I mean is, how can you best command the attention of those you are speaking to?” Pat once said. “Should you employ high decibels or low? Lesson 3 of 8
Situation

Heading

The second component of personal communication is being able to appropriately assess each unique situation to determine the right level of communication.
“Frequently, knowing what to say to someone is all about time and location,” Pat once said. “You don’t always make the right call. There’s a judgment involved. You have to ask yourself, ‘What does this person need today?’ And you have to watch his or her body language.”

(Download the transcript below)

Context of the Communication

Understanding the context of a conversation includes not only the physical setting but also the emotional backdrop of the communication.

Knowing Your Audience

Audience awareness is at the heart of situational communication. Different audiences require different approaches, vocabulary, and levels of formality.

Timing of the Communication

Timing can significantly influence communication effectiveness. Not every moment is ideal for every type of message; situational communicators recognize when to wait and when to act.

Nonverbal Communication

Body language, eye contact, posture, gestures and facial expressions—plays an equally important role in situational communication. Research shows that a large portion of human communication is non-verbal, meaning that words alone do not fully capture the message being conveyed. The non-verbal cues of the receiver can also help you gauge how your communication is being received. Are they sitting with their arms crossed? Scowling? etc.

The point is, context can significantly affect how a message is received.We’ll go over this more in the upcoming lesson.

Lesson 6: Pat’s Communication Style 
Michelle Marciniak 
You had to be receptive to her style of communication. Sometimes it was maybe aggressive and 
came across very strong and forceful. But that's what made Pat so successful. She was a very 
direct communicator. She communicated in a black and white style, meaning there was very 
little gray area, so you knew exactly where she stood at all times. And as an athlete, as a 
student athlete, you had to figure out what you wanted to do with that. And if you didn't know, 
she would also help you through that as well. 
There's no ambiguity. She's very direct. You know where you stand. And you don't walk out of 
the gym or in a meeting or film session and think, ‘Wow, I have no idea how I did or how I 
preformed.’

Lesson 5 of 8
Nonverbal

Listen to leadership coach Christina Gradillas give practical tips on improving tone and nonverbal communication habits.

(Download the transcript below)

Heading

Pat once told a story of how the 1977 team had stayed up late one night drinking and partying until 4 a.m. in violation of team policies. When they showed up for practice the next day completely hungover, she debated how to respond. She considered giving them a tongue lashing but thought the better of it. Instead, she put trash cans on the baseline at the corners of the gym and conducted practice for four hours, by the end of which almost every player had vomited into one of the trash cans.
Her point was made.

“If all you ever do is yell, then you will be heard less and less,” she said. “That’s why sometimes, saying nothing at all can be just as powerful.”
One of Pat’s famous mannerisms is the “Summitt Stare” — a famous glare she often employed on the sidelines. The stare is said to have been so intense that it could make players and officials alike feel nervous or unsettled. Players and opponents knew that when they saw the stare, they were in for a tough game.

As a coach, Pat knew when to speak and when to be silent. The habit of communicating through body language is one that the best communicators have intentionally worked on over time, choosing which postures, attitude, or gestures to use in which situation so they convey their message in the most effective way.

In the video above, listen to Michelle Marciniak, CEO of SHEEX and former WNBA player recall Pat’s emphasis on maintaining good eye contact.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 6: Tone and Nonverbal Communication 
Christina Gradillas 
Tone of voice is powerful when it comes to mastering the art of communication. How many 
times has a situation escalated simply because of the tone of voice? We all, male or female, fall 
prone to this, betraying our emotions when speaking or raising our voice when we don't mean 
to, when we get excited. There's nothing wrong with emotion. Don't get me wrong. Good 
leaders, skilled communicators, know how to master their emotion and be mindful of their 
tone. Pat Summit knew when to raise her voice during a game, but she also knew when to bring 
it down and remain calm. 
Okay, where are you in the area of body language? Pat once said, there is more to being vocal 
than simply being audible, especially if you are in a leadership role. You communicate with 
gestures and body language all the time without realizing it. How you sit in a meeting may send 
a message. Which chair you choose to sit in might send one also. You can unconsciously project 
confidence or uncertainty. “Generally, I don't sit on the sidelines. I stand because I feel closer to 
the game. Also, I'm aware that my body sends a message from 90 feet away. Good eye contact, 
a straight posture, and a thumbs up can impart conviction. It's not enough to say, I'm confident. 
You can say those words 100 times over and over, but no one will buy it if your shoulders are 
slumped and your voice cracks.” 
It turns out when it comes to success with professional body language, your mother was right. 
Stand up straight. Don't fidget. Smile and give a firm handshake. One way you can start to learn 
this is simply by observing others. Have you ever intentionally noticed this before? Who in your 
office has great body language? Take some time after this video to jot down a few people who 
come to mind. Now, why is this? What are they doing that sets them apart? Maybe they always 
appear cheerful and confident. Maybe it's the way they give you their full attention when 
someone is talking. Maybe they mimic your expressions to show they're with you when you're 
explaining something. It could be a variety of different things, but be intentional. Be on the 
lookout this week in your office. 
There are several books or videos out there that can help you work on your body language, but 
there are just a few techniques: 
• Good posture, not slouching, right? Not crossing your arms and looking closed off. No 
one wants to approach you like that. 
• Avoiding any nervous gestures like jiggling your leg or playing with your jewelry. 
• Face the person talking to you or lean in when they're speaking to show interest. 
• Proper use of your hands, not overdoing it or underdoing it with the hand motions.

It's hard to find someone who is a master at body language. We all have our unique quirks and 
traits, so it's important to figure out what yours are. And to do this, you may need a little bit of 
help. Have you ever watched yourself on a home movie and been horrified? Me too. Do I really 
talk like that? Do I really sound like that? You know who you are. So you want to do an audit 
where you are in the realm of body language. What are your strengths and what are your 
weaknesses? You also want to do the same for your facial expressions. It's easier than ever to 
see this now in the world of Zoom calls, but you may want to call in a friend or colleague you 
trust for backup. Tell them you're working on your body language and would they give you an 
honest opinion on two things you can improve. Or to let you know when your face is betraying 
you. And you'd be surprised at how many times our face is communicating something entirely 
different than what we think it is. You may have an expressive face, in which case every 
emotion, concern, frustration, anger, disappointment is visible on your face. Or you may have 
the opposite problem, a poker face, where there's little to no expression on your face and your 
coworkers can't read you that well. They may think on your face, and your coworkers can't read 
you that well. They may think you're displeased when you're not, or unfriendly when you're 
not. So, start with your face. 
You also want to be mindful of your eye contact. This may come very natural to you, but 
sometimes we can be naturally shy, perceived as less confident. If you're an introvert, male or 
female, good eye contact may not come naturally. A good rule of thumb is to make eye contact 
50% of the time when speaking, and 70% when listening. That's right, 70% when listening. 
If you find yourself struggling with eye contact at first, practice noticing the color of people's 
eyes. Hold eye contact for several seconds, as long as it takes to determine the color of their 
eyes. Then look away if you need to. If looking people in the eye is too stressful, look at the spot 
right between their eyes or their nose. Whatever it takes to start building the habit. 
Another technique to try is reading people's expression by looking only at their eyes. You'd be 
surprised by what someone's eyes can tell you. Do the eyes look sad? Tired? Excited? Nervous? 
There's a reason they say the eyes are the window to the soul. You'll find that in the process of 
trying to read people's eyes, you're working two skills: holding eye contact and learning to read 
other people's body language, which is a key part of emotional intelligence. 
So, that's several things to work on, but it's worth it. And even the greats still have to work on 
their body language and overall communication. In her memoir, Pat once wrote that she didn't 
consider herself starting off to be a very good communicator. “I was pretty helpless. It's a 
change I'm proud to have made, and it's the way in which I've grown most as a coach.” 
With all of that in mind, how will you grow?

gestures and body language all the time without realizing it. How you sit in a meeting may send 
a message. Which chair you choose to sit in might send one also. You can unconsciously project 
confidence or uncertainty. “Generally, I don't sit on the sidelines. I stand because I feel closer to 
the game. Also, I'm aware that my body sends a message from 90 feet away. Good eye contact, 
a straight posture, and a thumbs up can impart conviction. It's not enough to say, I'm confident. 
You can say those words 100 times over and over, but no one will buy it if your shoulders are 
slumped and your voice cracks.” 
It turns out when it comes to success with professional body language, your mother was right. 
Stand up straight. Don't fidget. Smile and give a firm handshake. One way you can start to learn 
this is simply by observing others. Have you ever intentionally noticed this before? Who in your 
office has great body language? Take some time after this video to jot down a few people who 
come to mind. Now, why is this? What are they doing that sets them apart? Maybe they always 
appear cheerful and confident. Maybe it's the way they give you their full attention when 
someone is talking. Maybe they mimic your expressions to show they're with you when you're 
explaining something. It could be a variety of different things, but be intentional. Be on the 
lookout this week in your office. 
There are several books or videos out there that can help you work on your body language, but 
there are just a few techniques: 
• Good posture, not slouching, right? Not crossing your arms and looking closed off. No 
one wants to approach you like that. 
• Avoiding any nervous gestures like jiggling your leg or playing with your jewelry. 
• Face the person talking to you or lean in when they're speaking to show interest. 
• Proper use of your hands, not overdoing it or underdoing it with the hand motions.

It's hard to find someone who is a master at body language. We all have our unique quirks and 
traits, so it's important to figure out what yours are. And to do this, you may need a little bit of 
help. Have you ever watched yourself on a home movie and been horrified? Me too. Do I really 
talk like that? Do I really sound like that? You know who you are. So you want to do an audit 
where you are in the realm of body language. What are your strengths and what are your 
weaknesses? You also want to do the same for your facial expressions. It's easier than ever to 
see this now in the world of Zoom calls, but you may want to call in a friend or colleague you 
trust for backup. Tell them you're working on your body language and would they give you an 
honest opinion on two things you can improve. Or to let you know when your face is betraying 
you. And you'd be surprised at how many times our face is communicating something entirely 
different than what we think it is. You may have an expressive face, in which case every 
emotion, concern, frustration, anger, disappointment is visible on your face. Or you may have 
the opposite problem, a poker face, where there's little to no expression on your face and your 
coworkers can't read you that well. They may think on your face, and your coworkers can't read 
you that well. They may think you're displeased when you're not, or unfriendly when you're 
not. So, start with your face. 
You also want to be mindful of your eye contact. This may come very natural to you, but 
sometimes we can be naturally shy, perceived as less confident. If you're an introvert, male or 
female, good eye contact may not come naturally. A good rule of thumb is to make eye contact 
50% of the time when speaking, and 70% when listening. That's right, 70% when listening. 
If you find yourself struggling with eye contact at first, practice noticing the color of people's 
eyes. Hold eye contact for several seconds, as long as it takes to determine the color of their 
eyes. Then look away if you need to. If looking people in the eye is too stressful, look at the spot 
right between their eyes or their nose. Whatever it takes to start building the habit. 
Another technique to try is reading people's expression by looking only at their eyes. You'd be 
surprised by what someone's eyes can tell you. Do the eyes look sad? Tired? Excited? Nervous? 
There's a reason they say the eyes are the window to the soul. You'll find that in the process of 
trying to read people's eyes, you're working two skills: holding eye contact and learning to read 
other people's body language, which is a key part of emotional intelligence. 
So, that's several things to work on, but it's worth it. And even the greats still have to work on 
their body language and overall communication. In her memoir, Pat once wrote that she didn't 
consider herself starting off to be a very good communicator. “I was pretty helpless. It's a 
change I'm proud to have made, and it's the way in which I've grown most as a coach.” 
With all of that in mind, how will you grow?

Lesson 6: The Power of Eye Contact 
Michelle Marciniak 
Pat was a great communicator. She was very strict, very stern. She wanted you to keep eye 
contact 24/7. If you looked away when she was talking to you, she would literally follow your 
eyes.  
Pat was an incredible communicator. She definitely knew how to get the best out of her 
players. 
So, what I learned from Pat: 
I think eye contact. Really, you get the feel for what people are thinking, why they're thinking it. 
So I think that's critical. 
Definitely, as an entrepreneur, try to maintain as much eye contact as possible, whether you're 
being interviewed or in an interview. That eye contact displays confidence. It displays like I'm 
here in this room and I mean something. And there's some kind of power in eye contact.

Lesson 7 of 8
Practice Makes Perfect

Heading

Finally, all three of these communication principles — tone, situation, and nonverbal communication — take lifelong practice. Your skills will evolve as you do in your role, and new situations will constantly present themselves. You never reach the finish line of perfect communication, but with a little awareness and intentionality, you can make sure you’re prepared to communicate wisely and effectively in any situation.

(Download the transcript below)

Listen to Michelle Marciniak remember a one-on-one pep talk from Pat on the importance of communication.

Each situation requires a different tone. We all know people who yell at every opportunity. They yell in the office, at home, in a restaurant. After a while, we tune them out. Too much of one thing tends to dull your listener’s sensibilities.”

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 6: You're Going to Have to Get Over That 
Michelle Marciniak 
When I first got to Tennessee, we had a team meeting and, you know, you walk into this 
amazing locker room and you sit down with all the rest of your teammates and it's the very first 
meeting. And Pat was obviously in the front of the room explaining what the notebook was on 
the table in front of us. And it said, Pat's definite dozen. And the Definite Dozen was not only 
Definite Dozen, but it was like the rules and regulations. And it was this thick. It was very thick. 
And so, you know, she starts going through like, you know, about eye contact and you'll be to 
class on time in the first three rows and like typical Pat fashion. So she goes through the 
Definite Dozen and why they're important and talks about how people that go before you, that 
have come before you, meaning the whole Title IX stories, she used that as an example of 
people that have paved the way for you before you even were able to sit in this really plush, 
nice locker room. 
She goes, and you will be leaders on and off the court. You have a responsibility to speak. You 
have a responsibility to introduce yourself, to be confident young women at all times. You'll 
sign autographs to fans, to the University of Tennessee, to the state of Tennessee, the city of 
Knoxville. 
So, then she said, again, you'll have to introduce yourself. So I sort of froze at this moment 
because what she didn't know and what nobody knew except me is that I grew up with a 
stuttering problem. And so I and I was made fun of terribly and I just didn't really know how to 
like work my way through that. And I just wanted to play basketball. But when she said, you'll 
stand up, you'll be a leader, you'll introduce yourself, you'll all this kind of stuff. I just started 
and I totally zoned out everything else that was happening. 
So that being the backstory, I went up to Pat after this meeting and I said, “Pat, I need to talk to 
you.” And she said, “When is your class tomorrow?” I said, “It's 8 a.m.” She goes, “Where is it?” 
And I say, “It's at the Hyper Building.” So she said, “I'll meet you on the track in the bleachers.” 
So 7.45, 7.30 comes. I meet Pat. She sits down next to me and she just looks at me and goes, 
“What's up?” And I mean, true Pat fashion. I said, “There's something I need to talk to you 
about.” And I think I think she may have thought, like, because of the serious tone in my body 
language, I think she thought that I was going to tell her I was like pregnant or like something 
like I can't do this. And this is why. No, I just said, “So I don't know exactly how to say this, but I 
have a stuttering problem and I have a fear of speaking. So like introducing myself and I said, 
that is extremely difficult for me and I don't like to do it. And it's not something that I don't 
think I can do.”

She just kind of looked at me very, very perplexed and said, “Is that all?” And I said, “Yeah, 
that's it.” She looked out on the track. She looks back at me and goes, “Well, you're going to 
have to get over that.” She patted me on the knee twice, you know, like a parent would and like 
pats me on the shoulder and says, “All right, get to class.” That was it. That was the extent of 
the interaction. 
This struggle that I've had my whole life speaking, I've had to always get over it. And that was a 
probably a really great learning. I didn't like her for it, but it was a great turning point for me to 
have the courage to face your fears. And for me, it was always it's always been speaking and to 
face your fears and just sort of tackle whatever you're scared of head-on and get over it.

Lesson 6: Transparency 
Corrine Milien 
When I think of communication, a story that often comes to mind is the time when Pat was 
announcing her illness. And it was very early in the season. We hadn't even started the season 
yet. We had freshmen just on campus. 
And it was very important that the players heard it from her. She didn't want the Knoxville 
News. She didn't want ESPN. She didn't want parents or anyone telling her players her story. So, 
I had to round up all these players, find them wherever they were, and bring them to the office 
so that Pat had the time, the transparency to communicate what was going on. 
And I think the players really appreciated that. They appreciated that she cared enough about 
what they thought in that moment to make the time to let them know what she was going 
through and what they could expect over the next year.

Lesson 1 of 9
Different Strokes, Different Folks 

(Download the transcript below)

Heading

It’s a fact of life: Not all people communicate in the same way, and it's important to understand different personality types and adjust your own communication style accordingly. Each personality type has its own style, preferences, and tendencies, and if you fail to adjust your approach, you may end up inadvertently alienating a team member.

For example, let's say you’re very direct and assertive, and you’re communicating with someone who is more reserved. If you come on too strong and don't take the time to listen to their perspective, you may make them feel intimidated. On the other hand, if you’re too passive and don't express your opinions clearly, the other person may perceive you as indecisive.

Communicating differently to different types can help you build stronger relationships and encourage greater understanding. When you tailor your approach to fit another person’s needs, you can help them feel valued and respected.

In another example, let's say you’re working on a team project with someone who is very detail-oriented and analytical. You may find that they prefer to receive information in a highly structured and organized format, even though this isn’t your style. By taking the time to present your ideas in a clear and logical way, you can help them feel more comfortable and engaged in the process.

It’s a question of personalities and finding the most effective language to use with a player. Some people, you can rip their heads off, and they still won’t give you their full attention. Others will break at a single word.”

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 7: Different Strokes, Different Folks 
Danni Varlan 
Raise your hand if you know someone in your life who either communicates or receives 
communication differently than you do. We all do, right? Sometimes they live with us. 
Sometimes we're related to them. And sometimes we're raising them. And the workplace is no 
different. 
When she was coaching her players, Pat famously said, "It's a question of personalities and 
finding the most effective language to use with a player." Some people you can rip their heads 
off and they still won't give you their full attention. Others will break at a single word. Do you 
know the personality types of those you work with? Could you guess? Take a minute after this 
video to jot down the names of your team members along with a simple word or tag beside 
their name: 
• Extrovert 
• Introvert 
• Thinker 
• Feeler 
These four words go a long way in telling you how to communicate with others. But we often 
don't even slow down to think about it, much less the more detailed parts of each personality.  
If you gave a personality test to each member of your team, chances are they would be unique 
flowers with different facets and elements to their personality. So you can't really walk around 
doing learning style tests with everybody you meet. But there are a few tips that you can use to 
sort of figure out what it might be. For example, do they like to learn through people and 
experience? Or do they like to learn through books and experts? And after they learn 
something, do they want to just go do it? Or do they want to think about it for a while and get it 
right in their head before they decide to start? 
So how does that help you as a leader? Well, this carries over to how you as a leader choose to 
communicate in any given situation with a particular team member. 
Take Tamara, an assertive go-getter. Let's say Tamara's driven, confident, and results-oriented. 
When communicating with someone like Tamara, be direct and concise. Respect her time and 
get to the point quickly. Emphasize facts and outcomes. She may appreciate evidence to 
support your ideas. Stay professional. Keep emotions in check and focus on the task at hand. 
Now let's meet Mark, a friendly social butterfly. Mark is outgoing, extroverted, and loves to 
connect with others. When communicating with someone like Mark, engage in small talk. Take

a few minutes to ask about his weekend or hobbies. Slow down and be approachable. Be an 
active listener. Show interest in what he has to say and be sure you're practicing active 
listening. 
Or Juan, the analytical perfectionist. Juan is detail-oriented, precise, and values accuracy. When 
communicating with someone like Juan, present data. Support your ideas with well-researched 
information. Be patient and open to questions. Juan may need time to process and seek clarity. 
Do you have any people like this on your team? I bet you do. Another really good example is my 
husband and me. We are the total opposite. I am always ready to do something out, very, very 
social, and he is very quiet. He wants to know all of the details and he wants to think about it. 
And think about it. And think about it. Until he gets the right answer. 
This information can be used anywhere. So, let's get started in learning how you can become a 
master in using different communication strokes for different folks.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: It’s a fact of life: Not all people communicate in the same way, and it's important to understand different personality types and adjust your own communication style accordingly. Each personality type has its own style, preferences, and tendencies, and if you fail to adjust your approach, you may end up inadvertently alienating a team member.

For example, let's say you’re very direct and assertive, and you’re communicating with someone who is more reserved. If you come on too strong and don't take the time to listen to their perspective, you may make them feel intimidated. On the other hand, if you’re too passive and don't express your opinions clearly, the other person may perceive you as indecisive.

Communicating differently to different types can help you build stronger relationships and encourage greater understanding. When you tailor your approach to fit another person’s needs, you can help them feel valued and respected.

In another example, let's say you’re working on a team project with someone who is very detail-oriented and analytical. You may find that they prefer to receive information in a highly structured and organized format, even though this isn’t your style. By taking the time to present your ideas in a clear and logical way, you can help them feel more comfortable and engaged in the process.

items.name: — Pat Summitt
items.paragraph: It’s a question of personalities and finding the most effective language to use with a player. Some people, you can rip their heads off, and they still won’t give you their full attention. Others will break at a single word.”

Lesson 3 of 9
Extroverts vs. Introverts

One of the simplest differences in personality styles is extroverts vs. introverts. Extroverts are outgoing, talkative, and enjoy being around other people. They often think out loud and process information verbally. In contrast, introverts are more reserved and introspective. They tend to think before they speak and may need time to process information internally. To communicate effectively with extroverts, try to engage them in conversation and give them opportunities to express their ideas. Use open-ended questions and active listening skills to show you’re interested in what they have to say.

On the other hand, to communicate effectively with introverts, try to give them space and time to process information. Give them clear, concise instructions and allow them to work independently. For example, if you are working with an introverted colleague, you might send them an email outlining the project requirements and asking them to review the information before meeting to discuss further. This can give them the time they need to think through their ideas and come to the conversation prepared.

Exercise

Drag and drop each behavior into the appropriate column, depending on whether it works best for introverts or extroverts.

Allowing uninterrupted focus time, with a quiet place to work

Starting each meeting off with icebreaker questions

Encouraging daily face-to-face interactions among the team

Providing clear directions and allowing team members to work independently

Sending meeting agendas in advance with lots of detail

Planning extra social activities outside of project meetings

Avoiding calling on team members on the spot in meetings

Introverts

Extroverts

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 4 of 9
Thinkers vs. Feelers

Heading

Another difference is between “thinkers” and “feelers.” Thinkers are logical and analytical. They prefer to focus on facts and data and may have a more detached approach to problem-solving. Feelers, on the other hand, are more emotional and empathetic. They are focused on relationships and may prioritize the feelings and needs of others.

To communicate effectively with thinkers, try to provide them with clear, data-driven information. Use objective language and avoid emotional appeals. If you are presenting an idea to a group of thinkers, you might start by providing them with a data-driven analysis of the situation and the potential benefits of your idea. You can then invite questions and discussion to help them explore the idea more deeply.

On the other hand, to communicate effectively with feelers, try to acknowledge their emotions and show empathy for their perspective. Use language that highlights the potential impact on people and relationships. If you’re presenting an idea to a group of feelers, you might start by acknowledging the emotional impact of the situation and how your idea could help improve the situation. You can then invite questions and discussion to help them explore the idea more deeply from an emotional perspective.

Lesson 5 of 9
Personality Testing

Heading

To go beyond the general assessments of “introvert-extrovert” or “thinker-feeler,” you can also gain insight into personality types through personality trait assessments. Pat famously used the Predictive Index assessment with her players in the 1990s, relying on the tool to understand each player’s natural motivations. But there are many tools and assessments to choose from nowadays.

Types of Personality Tests

Here are a few of the more common tools you may find in the space.
(Scroll through to complete this element)

Summary

Consider what personality trait assessment tool might work best for your team members, and how you can share those results with the team.

Predictive Index (PI)

The Predictive Index (PI) is based on the theory of behavioral drives, which suggests that individuals have innate needs that drive their behavior in the workplace. It measures four primary personality factors:
Dominance – the drive to exert influence and control over one's environment
Extraversion – the drive to interact with and gain energy from one's environment
Patience – the drive to maintain stability and consistency in one's environment
Formality – the drive to conform to rules and structure in one's environment
Based on an individual's responses to the PI assessment, their scores on these four factors are plotted on a grid that generates a personality profile. The profile helps predict their leadership style, communication style, decision-making approach, and ability to work independently or as part of a team. For example, an individual with a high Dominance score is likely to be assertive and confident, while someone with a high Patience score may prefer a steady and predictable environment.

Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI)

The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator is a personality trait assessment that measures an individual's preferences on four dimensions: Extraversion vs. Introversion, Sensing vs. Intuition, Thinking vs. Feeling, and Judging vs. Perceiving. Based on these preferences, an individual is assigned one of 16 possible personality types, such as ISTJ (Introverted, Sensing, Thinking, Judging) or ENFP (Extraverted, Intuitive, Feeling, Perceiving). Knowing an individual's MBTI type can help you understand their communication style and how they generally prefer to receive information, in addition to other personality insights.

The Enneagram

The Enneagram is a personality assessment that categorizes individuals into nine different personality types based on their core fears, desires, and motivations. These types include the Reformer, the Helper, the Achiever, the Individualist, the Investigator, the Loyalist, the Enthusiast, the Challenger, and the Peacemaker. Understanding an individual's Enneagram type can help you understand their underlying motivations and needs. For example, a Peacemaker may prioritize harmony and avoiding conflict, while someone with an Enthusiast type might prioritize relationships and fun.

DISC Profile

The DISC profile is another traditionally used personality trait assessment that measures an individual's Dominance, Influence, Steadiness, and Conscientiousness. These factors are plotted on a graph to generate a personality profile that can help predict an individual's communication style and behavior in different situations with a percentage given for each type.

Big Five Personality Traits

The Big Five personality traits are a set of five broad dimensions that are used to describe human personality. These traits include Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism. Understanding an individual's Big Five personality traits can help you understand their communication style, values, and preferences. An individual with a high Openness score may be more creative and open to new ideas, while someone with a high Conscientiousness score might prioritize organization and planning.

StrengthsFinder

StrengthsFinder is a personality trait assessment that measures an individual's top five unique strengths across 34 different themes, such as Strategic, Achiever, Empathy, or Adaptability. Understanding an individual's strengths can help you communicate with them in a way that acknowledges their unique skills and abilities in the workplace.

Hogan Personality Inventory (HPI)

The Hogan Personality Inventory is a personality trait assessment that measures an individual's personality in terms of three main categories: Reputation, Identity, and Motives. Reputation refers to how an individual is perceived by others, Identity refers to how an individual sees themselves, and Motives refers to the underlying drivers of an individual's behavior. Understanding an individual's HPI profile can help you understand their communication style, their strengths, and their potential weaknesses.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 7: The Importance of Learning Styles 
Danni Varlan 
In 2000, I was the program director for a leadership program and Pat invited us to come over 
and do a learning styles assessment with her players. We were very excited about that, as you 
can imagine, and were very surprised to find out what everybody's learning style was, as well as 
Pat. 
But the fun part about it was as we did it, she learned some skills that were going to give her an 
opportunity for communicating better with several of her players. One in particular was just 
very kind, very nice, loved people, but wanted everybody to be happy. So sometimes that got in 
the way of a perfect shot and she would stop and pass it off to someone. So, and you know, Pat 
just wasn't crazy about that. So this was giving her an opportunity to learn how she could more 
effectively communicate with this player. 
On the other hand, she had another player that was a great point guard and she was skilled and 
was very comfortable making decisions on the fly. In fact, at the end of every game, she would 
write a three-page legal pad and give Pat her assessment of that game. 
Now with her staff, she also found out some very interesting information. You know, 
sometimes there would be a good cop, bad cop scenario with the team and it became very 
clear who was going to play what role when they did learning styles. But it also became clear in 
terms of how comfortable they were with certain subjects with their teams. 
So, learning styles became a part of Pat's everyday involvement with her team and actually in 
her life. She was very interested in how people wanted to communicate and how to best 
communicate with them.

Based on these preferences, an individual is assigned one of 16 possible personality types, such as ISTJ (Introverted, Sensing, Thinking, Judging) or ENFP (Extraverted, Intuitive, Feeling, Perceiving). Knowing an individual's MBTI type can help you understand their communication style and how they generally prefer to receive information, in addition to other personality insights.

The Enneagram | The Enneagram is a personality assessment that categorizes individuals into nine different personality types based on their core fears, desires, and motivations. These types include the Reformer, the Helper, the Achiever, the Individualist, the Investigator, the Loyalist, the Enthusiast, the Challenger, and the Peacemaker. Understanding an individual's Enneagram type can help you understand their underlying motivations and needs. For example, a Peacemaker may prioritize harmony and avoiding conflict, while someone with an Enthusiast type might prioritize relationships and fun.

DISC Profile | The DISC profile is another traditionally used personality trait assessment that measures an individual's Dominance, Influence, Steadiness, and Conscientiousness. These factors are plotted on a graph to generate a personality profile that can help predict an individual's communication style and behavior in different situations with a percentage given for each type.

Big Five Personality Traits | The Big Five personality traits are a set of five broad dimensions that are used to describe human personality. These traits include Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism. Understanding an individual's Big Five personality traits can help you understand their communication style, values, and preferences. An individual with a high Openness score may be more creative and open to new ideas, while someone with a high Conscientiousness score might prioritize organization and planning.

StrengthsFinder | StrengthsFinder is a personality trait assessment that measures an individual's top five unique strengths across 34 different themes, such as Strategic, Achiever, Empathy, or Adaptability. Understanding an individual's strengths can help you communicate with them in a way that acknowledges their unique skills and abilities in the workplace.

Hogan Personality Inventory (HPI) | The Hogan Personality Inventory is a personality trait assessment that measures an individual's personality in terms of three main categories: Reputation, Identity, and Motives. Reputation refers to how an individual is perceived by others, Identity refers to how an individual sees themselves, and Motives refers to the underlying drivers of an individual's behavior. Understanding an individual's HPI profile can help you understand their communication style, their strengths, and their potential weaknesses.

items.paragraph: To go beyond the general assessments of “introvert-extrovert” or “thinker-feeler,” you can also gain insight into personality types through personality trait assessments. Pat famously used the Predictive Index assessment with her players in the 1990s, relying on the tool to understand each player’s natural motivations. But there are many tools and assessments to choose from nowadays.

items.title: Predictive Index (PI)
items.description:
The Predictive Index (PI) is based on the theory of behavioral drives, which suggests that individuals have innate needs that drive their behavior in the workplace. It measures four primary personality factors:

Dominance – the drive to exert influence and control over one's environment

Extraversion – the drive to interact with and gain energy from one's environment

Patience – the drive to maintain stability and consistency in one's environment

Formality – the drive to conform to rules and structure in one's environment

Based on an individual's responses to the PI assessment, their scores on these four factors are plotted on a grid that generates a personality profile. The profile helps predict their leadership style, communication style, decision-making approach, and ability to work independently or as part of a team. For example, an individual with a high Dominance score is likely to be assertive and confident, while someone with a high Patience score may prefer a steady and predictable environment.

Lesson 7 of 9
Criticism and Praise

Heading

Finally, when learning to communicate with different personality types, one principle Pat always believed in was supplementing any necessary criticisms with praise and knowing how to use both wisely.

When is it appropriate to use harsh words? Only you can be the judge of that. But I’ll say this: They must be used in combination with praise. Negative reinforcement must be used sparingly.”

(Please listen to complete this element)

Click to hear the quote above.

Realizing that praise was necessary to keep her team going as well as the routine critiques and criticisms, Pat developed a system called “rebound and two points” to help her players remember the use of both. Whenever an opportunity for improvement or chastisement was issued, the player would say, “Rebound!” to show they understood and knew the criticism was for the best. When praise was given, they were to say, “Two points!” to indicate that they heard the praise and it had been received. The verbal reinforcement was necessary, Pat believed, to ensure the players weren’t hearing and internalizing only the criticism.

In summary, whether using praise or criticism, communicating with extroverts, introverts, or other diverse personalities, using the right communication style can make all the difference. The next time you're in a conversation with someone, take a moment to consider their communication style and adjust your approach accordingly. You might be surprised at how much more effective your communication becomes.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 7: Slowing Down to Interact with Fans 
Alexis Hornbuckle 
Coach Summitt was a big influence in my life, and it wasn't just because she was strict and I told 
my dad the reason I wanted to go to Tennessee, this lady's crazy. She'll keep me in check. But 
beyond that, she was probably one of the most compassionate, nicest, motherly individuals you 
could ever meet. As college kids, you're just that, you're kids, who your parents entrust in the 
coach's hands. And she made sure to treat us all like her daughters. 
I mean, cookouts. By the way, Coach Summitt could throw down in the kitchen. That lady could 
cook her butt off, okay? And that just made it even better. That nice home-cooked meal served 
with a smile and making sure that everybody was well taken care of. Pat didn't miss a beat with 
that. When it came to the kids or the fans, she's signing every single autograph that she 
possibly can. She's taking every single picture that she possibly can. That's just to be who she 
was of her stature and to leave the legacy that she left. Even while she was alive and coaching, 
her legacy was already built. 
So to see someone like that who doesn't have to stop for photos, who doesn't have to stop for 
autographs, who doesn't have to stop just to have a conversation with the janitor, she was 
exactly that person. And I could tell you, it doesn't matter how big you get as an athlete, as a 
coach, as a leader, take the time. Take the time to just put a smile on someone's face and make 
their day. 
Coach used to be big on open door policy. I'm going to speak to everybody and everybody can 
speak to me. That is huge. Today it's a whole lot of egos, a whole lot of pride in a lot of 
positions. Coach wasn't that. And that woman won eight national championships. And she's 
legendary. I take note if I were you.

Lesson 1 of 7
Listening to Lead

(Download the transcript below)

Heading

A final step to becoming an excellent communicator that Pat always emphasized is the act of listening to lead. As a leader, listening is one of the most overlooked skills you can have. But what does it really mean to listen as a leader? Is it just about nodding your head and pretending to hear what your team is saying? Absolutely not. True listening is about connecting with your team on a deeper level and attempting to understand their perspectives and needs.

How many of us go through a day without saying a word? None of us. But maybe we ought to try it. Communicating is not just about giving great speeches. It’s about allowing others to express themselves.”

Lesson 8: Listening to Lead 
Steve Hamer 
As a coach, Pat Summitt was known for her commanding tone and strong leadership style. But 
did you know that she also spent a lot of time learning to listen? Listening well is one of the 
best kept secrets to being a leader. How many of us go through a day without saying a word? 
None of us. But maybe we ought to try it, she once said. Communicating is not just about giving 
great speeches, it's about allowing others to express themselves. If a championship coach like 
Pat Summitt can take the time to slow down and listen to those she was leading, you can too. 
One of the things that I have learned over the years, especially being a married man, is that 
there is a reason why we have two ears and one mouth. That means that we should listen twice 
as much as we should speak. For me, that has really resonated a great deal because as an 
effective leader, I want to make sure that I listen to everyone that I lead. Again, there is a 
difference between hearing and listening. Actively listening means that you are paying 
attention to what is being said, and you ingest what is being said, thus making you a more 
impactful leader. 
So, as I work every single day, I make sure that I put the needs of others before myself, 
especially when it comes to operating in the highest capacity. That means that I'm listening, I'm 
actively listening instead of just thinking of the next thing to say. As a leader, your ability to 
listen actively and sympathetically plays a significant role in encouraging a positive work 
environment, promoting collaboration, and ultimately achieving success. Listening is the 
foundation of building trust and respect on your team. 
When you actively listen to your employees, they feel value and it creates a sense of 
psychological safety. Take the time to engage in open conversations where employees feel 
comfortable expressing their thoughts and concerns. By valuing their feedback, you are 
demonstrating that their contributions matter to the team. Rather than simply having everyone 
feel heard, understanding your team's needs and concerns is essential for having the 
knowledge to effectively address potential issues proactively as a leader. 
And how you listen is just as important as the act of listening itself. No lesson on 
communication would be complete without a closer look at this important topic. So, take a 
breath and let's learn more on how you can become an active listener in the workplace.

Lesson 2 of 7
Listening as a Leader

Heading

Now, we know what you're thinking. I already have too much on my plate. Who has time to listen? Well, my friend, if you don't make the time to listen to your team, you're going to have a lot more on your plate in the long run. Trust us.

So, let's talk about what it means to listen as a leader. First and foremost, it means being present. That means putting down your phone, closing your laptop, and actually looking at the person speaking to you. But listening isn't just about being physically present — it's also about being mentally present. That means clearing your mind of distractions and focusing on what the person is saying. That can be tough. Sometimes, it feels like our minds are like a web browser with dozens of tabs open at once. But just like how we close some tabs to avoid a crash, we need to focus on one thing at a time to avoid a “mental crash.”

As a leader, your job isn't to have all the answers. It's to help your team find the answers themselves. That means listening to their ideas and helping them think through solutions. And if they come up with a solution that's different from what you would have done, that's OK. In fact, it might even be better. Leaders who are too afraid to listen to their teams risk stifling creativity and innovation.
“Often a strong, dominant leader is the worst listener. He or she is too busy telling everyone else what to do and what to think,” Pat once noted.1

As a leader, it's important to listen to your employees. Not only does it make them feel valued and respected, but it also helps you make more informed decisions.
Active listening is a technique that involves concentrating on what someone is saying and being fully present. Passive listening is when the listener isn’t actively engaging in the conversation. The listener may be physically present, but their mind is elsewhere.
Please click each to complete this element.

Giving someone your undivided attention

Active Listening

Allowing distractions to interfere or disengaging

Passive Listening

While you are listening to someone, don’t just take in the words. Study the speaker. Be aware of the speaker’s voice and mannerisms. Notice what his or her effect is on you. Be aware of your own voice and body language, too.”

Lesson 4 of 7
Having 1:1 Conversations

Scroll through to complete this element.

Set Aside Time for 1:1 Conversations

One-on-one conversations are a great way to get to know your employees on a personal level and understand their perspective. As your schedule allows, make it a priority to work them into your regular routine.
Here are some tips to make the most of the time in your 1:1s.

Summary

Consider which of these you can work in to meetings with your team to help model active listening the most.

Avoid distractions.

When you're having a conversation with an employee, avoid distractions like checking your phone or looking at your computer. Give them your undivided attention.

Ask open-ended questions.

Open-ended questions can help you get a better understanding of your employee's perspective. Ask questions like, "How do you feel about this situation?" or "What do you think we can do to improve?"

Don't interrupt.

Interrupting someone when they’re speaking makes them feel like their opinions aren’t valued. Wait until they have finished speaking before responding.

Take notes.

Taking notes during a conversation shows the other person that you’re taking their concerns seriously and you value their input. It also helps you remember important details.

Be empathetic.

Empathy is the ability to understand and share someone else's feelings. When you're listening to an employee, try to put yourself in their shoes and understand how they are feeling.

Repeat/confirm the issue.

To show the speaker you understand the issue being communicated and to avoid any miscommunication, listen to the employee as they share, then repeat back the problem or issue being discussed. (“Just to make sure I understand, you’re saying the problem is with the new supply chain. Is that the issue?”) This shows the employee that you’re listening and gives them a chance to clarify any additional details if needed. (“Yes, it’s mainly the supply chain, but there’s also an issue with the details on the packages out of the Denver office.”)

Follow up.

After a conversation, follow up with your employee to let them know that you have taken their concerns into consideration. This helps build trust and shows that you are committed to addressing their concerns.

Lesson 5 of 7
Knowledge Check

Why is it important to set aside time for 1:1 conversations with your employees?

To understand their perspective and build trust

Setting aside time for 1:1 conversations helps you understand your employees' perspectives and builds trust by showing you value their input.

To delegate tasks more efficiently

While delegation is important, the primary purpose of 1:1 conversations is to connect with employees and understand their concerns.

To avoid distractions during team meetings

Avoiding distractions is a good practice during any meeting, but it is not the main reason for having 1:1 conversations.

To ensure employees follow company policies

1:1 conversations are not primarily about enforcing company policies but about understanding and supporting employees.

Which of the following is a key practice for active listening during a 1:1 conversation?

Avoiding distractions like checking your phone

Avoiding distractions ensures you give your full attention to the speaker, which is essential for active listening.

Interrupting to share your perspective

Interrupting can make the speaker feel undervalued and disrupts the flow of the conversation.

Taking a phone call during the conversation

Taking a phone call during a conversation is a distraction and demonstrates passive listening.

Focusing on formulating your response while the other person speaks

Focusing on your response instead of listening attentively can lead to missing important details.

Why is it important to follow up with an employee after a one-on-one conversation?

It shows that you value their input and are committed to addressing their concerns.

Following up demonstrates that you take their concerns seriously and helps build trust.

It allows you to avoid having future one-on-one conversations.

Avoiding future conversations does not foster trust or effective communication.

It ensures that the employee feels their opinions are not important.

This is incorrect as following up actually shows that their opinions are valued.

It gives you an opportunity to delegate their concerns to someone else.

Delegating concerns without addressing them yourself can undermine trust and accountability.

items.title: Why is it important to set aside time for 1:1 conversations with your employees?

answers.title: To understand their perspective and build trust
answers.feedback: Setting aside time for 1:1 conversations helps you understand your employees' perspectives and builds trust by showing you value their input.

answers.title: To delegate tasks more efficiently
answers.feedback: While delegation is important, the primary purpose of 1:1 conversations is to connect with employees and understand their concerns.

answers.title: To avoid distractions during team meetings
answers.feedback: Avoiding distractions is a good practice during any meeting, but it is not the main reason for having 1:1 conversations.

answers.title: To ensure employees follow company policies
answers.feedback: 1:1 conversations are not primarily about enforcing company policies but about understanding and supporting employees.

items.title: Which of the following is a key practice for active listening during a 1:1 conversation?

answers.title: Avoiding distractions like checking your phone
answers.feedback: Avoiding distractions ensures you give your full attention to the speaker, which is essential for active listening.

answers.title: Interrupting to share your perspective
answers.feedback: Interrupting can make the speaker feel undervalued and disrupts the flow of the conversation.

answers.title: Taking a phone call during the conversation
answers.feedback: Taking a phone call during a conversation is a distraction and demonstrates passive listening.

answers.title: Focusing on formulating your response while the other person speaks
answers.feedback: Focusing on your response instead of listening attentively can lead to missing important details.

items.title: Why is it important to follow up with an employee after a one-on-one conversation?

answers.title: It shows that you value their input and are committed to addressing their concerns.
answers.feedback: Following up demonstrates that you take their concerns seriously and helps build trust.

answers.title: It allows you to avoid having future one-on-one conversations.
answers.feedback: Avoiding future conversations does not foster trust or effective communication.

answers.title: It ensures that the employee feels their opinions are not important.
answers.feedback: This is incorrect as following up actually shows that their opinions are valued.

answers.title: It gives you an opportunity to delegate their concerns to someone else.
answers.feedback: Delegating concerns without addressing them yourself can undermine trust and accountability.

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 6 of 7
Create a Culture of Open Communication

Scroll through to complete this element.

Create a Culture of Open Communication

Encourage your employees to speak up and share their ideas by creating a culture of open communication.
Here are some things to keep in mind when encouraging openness.

Summary

In the end, listening as a leader is about creating a culture of openness and respect. It's about being willing to hear perspectives that are different from your own and using those perspectives to make better decisions. So, take the time to listen to your team — you might just be surprised by what you hear!

Seek regular feedback.

Asking your employees for feedback on your leadership style shows that you’re open to growth and improvement. It also helps you better understand their needs.

Don’t punish solicited feedback.

Even if feedback may be negative in nature, avoid punishing honest feedback that you asked for, as long as it’s given respectfully.

Thank them for sharing.

Thanking your employees for sharing their concerns or ideas shows that you value their input and appreciate their willingness to speak up.

Go on a listening tour.

To get a full sense of issues facing those you manage, once or twice a year go on a "listening tour" of your workplace to understand the perspectives and concerns of your team members. Make listening a conscious priority, whether by a series of structured feedback sessions or informal 1:1s. This helps uncover problems or feedback that may not arise solely through casual conversation.

Exercise

Which of these behaviors can leaders use to encourage open communication, versus closed communication?
Flip each card to complete this element.

Open! This allows communication to flow freely between teams.

Cross-department collaboration

Closed! When communication is unnecessarily siloed, it creates closed communication loops.

Emphasizing hierarchy

Open! This allows everyone to hear important communication from the source, in person.

Regular department meetings

Closed! If leaders respond negatively to mistakes, employees may avoid speaking up or for fear of criticism.

Emphasizing perfectionism

Open! This allows leaders to hear feedback, good news and concerns in an informal setting.

Walking the floor

Closed! Over-monitoring communication channels or tools stifles employees ability to speak freely when working.

Micromanaging communication channels

Open! When you share both the good and the bad with team members, it builds trust.

Sharing both good and bad news

Closed! If feedback is only solicited through forms or emails, communication will be stifled.

Discouraging informality

Lesson 7 of 7
Personal Reflections

(Download the transcript below)

Heading

Listen to Sr. Vice President Petra Dunn of Merrill Lynch remember her first meeting with Pat and how she prioritized listening.
Refer to your workbook for the reflection questions and exercises below.

How much do you currently practice listening as a leader? (Be honest!)

What percentage of your communication style involves actively communicating vs. actively listening?

Think about someone you know who was one of the worst listeners you’ve encountered. What traits did they have that made them this way?

Think about two individuals you know who are great listeners. What specific traits do each have?

Exercise

When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

Give yourself a grade for listening on a scale of 1 to 10.

Now, how good are you at active listening?

What are three things you can do to improve?1.2.3.

Take it to the next level: Ask a colleague you trust for their opinion on the question above. Continue to reflect.
What are three ways you can get better in each of your weaker areas?

Sources:
Unless otherwise noted, all quotes taken from, Reach for the Summitt, by Pat Summitt and Sally Jenkins. Three Rivers Press. 1998.

Congratulations!
That concludes this course. Please remember to close it before opening another course. You can revisit the completed course material at any time.

EXIT COURSE

Lesson 8: My First Meeting with Pat 
Petra Dunn 
I remember the first time I met Pat. I was so intimidated. She was a new client and I went to see 
her and here I am meeting with this legendary coach, coach of the century as a matter of fact, 
and I'm bringing her advice and guidance. 
And I was going into the meeting thinking she would pick everything apart and analyze every 
detail. And on the contrary, she was so humble and so respectful and recognized that she said, 
"Patria, you're the professional. I've got to trust you and what you tell me." 
It was really humbling for me because of the respect she gave. And it taught me to exemplify 
that in my own career and to the other people that I can mentor along the way. So, I thank her 
for that and giving me that feeling of just being the one in the room that she was able to just 
say, "You're the professional. I'm going to trust you." 
So that was a great memory for me.

Lesson 1 of 6
You Have to Demonstrate Loyalty to Receive It

(Download the transcript below)

Heading

Ah, employee loyalty. A lost art, right? With employees changing jobs every few years, people being more transient in general, and an ever-changing workplace, it feels like the days of 20- or 30-year employees and the “company” man or woman are gone.
This feeling isn’t completely unfounded. According to Forbes, the average tenure for an employee in recent years is around 4.1 years, offset by the fact that nearly 38 percent of employees quit within the first year.1 And why not?, you might ask. People have more options. People have more needs. There are more industries and companies than ever to choose from, and they’re more diverse.

Loyalty is a selfless proposition. You won’t ever have it unless you are willing to give it away first.”

(Please listen to complete this element)

Click play to hear the quote above.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 9: You Have to Demonstrate Loyalty to Receive It 
Joan Cronan 
In today's fast-paced world, businesses face fierce competition and constant challenges. And to 
thrive in such an environment, employees need to be dedicated and committed employees 
who share their vision and their values. Loyalty from employees translates into increased 
productivity, reduced turnover, and a competitive work culture. When employees feel valued 
and supported, they are more motivated to invest their skills and contribute meaningfully to 
the organization's success. They are also more likely to go the extra mile to be passionate 
ambassadors for the company. 
But despite its significance, loyalty seems to be a diminishing principle in today's workplace. In 
the pursuit of profit and growth, some organizations prioritize short-term gains over long-term 
relationships with employees. Downsizing, outsourcing, and frequent restructuring can leave 
employees feeling dispensable and undervalued. Similarly, employees may view employers 
primarily as steppingstones to advance their careers, leading to a lack of commitment and 
loyalty. 
So, how can we cultivate loyalty in the workplace? It begins with a two-way street of 
appreciation between employees and employers. Nurturing a loyal workforce requires creating 
a culture that values people over profit. Encouraging work-life balance, promoting employees' 
well-being, and offering flexibility are essential aspects of this. Employers can also demonstrate 
loyalty by providing: 
• Competitive compensation 
• Benefits 
• Opportunities for growth and development 
On the other hand, employees can exhibit loyalty by: 
• Maintaining a positive attitude 
• Operating with integrity 
• Avoiding gossip 
• Giving 100% on the job 
No matter what product or service you're offering, an organization is only as good as its people. 
Everything begins and ends with the people you have on your staff. Coach Summit knew this 
and prioritized loyalty highly among her favorite Definite Dozen leadership principles. You 
know, when I think of Pat and how she worked with her staff, it was incredible. Never, ever did 
she just assume they were there to help her. She always assumed that they were to work

together. You know, one time we won a championship and I was so excited that when we came 
back for the celebration, I was able to get a Mercedes for Pat to drive for a year for winning a 
championship. So we presented it at the celebration and everybody was thrilled. Well, the next 
year when Pat and I were visiting about if we might win a championship or when we would win 
a championship, she said, let's do something for our assistants. So I got a Mercedes for all three 
assistants because all of them had been there for the three previous championships. It was so 
much fun to watch Pat enjoy her assistants get excited. 
In short, loyalty in the workplace is not just an abstract concept, but a tangible force that 
influences an organization's success. By cultivating loyalty to employers and employees alike, 
we create an ecosystem of dedication that propels our businesses to new levels. Loyalty is not 
just about staying at an organization, but about profound commitment to thrive together.

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 3 of 6
Employee Turnover

Heading

The recent increase in employee turnover has led to a countering philosophy on the end of employers: Everyone is expendable. With full-time HR departments packed with recruiters, filling seats to replace empty ones has become a booming industry in itself. A new culture has emerged on behalf of the organization: Hire all the top talent you can find, and let nature take its course. We’ll do our best, but if people don’t like it, they can leave, and we’ll replace them with another highly paid person. No one’s really expecting team members to have loyalty, and the organization or company is not showing loyalty in return.

The kicker is… no one really likes this arrangement. Not the employee, not the employer. No matter how practical the hiring industry becomes, if you’re an employee, it can be exhausting to look for jobs every four years. If you’re an employer, it can cost up to 33 percent of an employee’s salary to replace the ones who leave ($15,000 for a $45,000 full-time position).2 Not to mention the impact it makes on an organization’s culture and employees’ sense of well-being.

On their end, employees have watched employers over-hire thousands of employees, then layoff thousands at a time to balance things out when the market corrects. Employees who do survive the layoffs often end up watching their colleagues being axed through emails with little notice, and are then asked to plod on, showing unquestioning loyalty to the company. Employers, by contrast, have scrambled to implement the best benefits programs and most flexible work arrangements available, only to watch their employee base hemorrhage through mass exoduses.

If you want to develop loyalty, the first thing you have to do is demonstrate it. Too many people use the term loyalty unilaterally. Especially bosses. They demand loyalty without reciprocating. They ask ‘Staff, have you been loyal to me?’ But what about the manager’s loyalty to the staff?”

(Please listen to complete this element)

Click play to hear the quote above.

Lesson 5 of 6
You Win in Life With People

Pat believed the single most common reason organizations self-destruct is disloyalty.
When asked about her championship teams, she famously said, “If you want to demonstrate loyalty, the first thing you have to do is demonstrate it. Too many people use the term loyalty unilaterally. Especially bosses. They demand loyalty without reciprocating. They ask ‘Staff, have you been loyal to me?’ But what about the manager’s loyalty to the staff?”3

Heading

In the upcoming lessons we’ll learn more on how to be loyal to your team, and how to be a leader no one will ever want to leave.

You win with people. I don’t care how good you are. I don’t care what kind of genius you may be. If you don’t have a good, loyal staff, you will not succeed.”

(Please listen to complete this element)

Click play to hear the quote above.

(Download the transcript below)

Listen to UT Associate Athletic Director Jimmy Delaney explain Pat’s personal philosophy that you win in life with people.
