Lesson 9: You Win in Life with People 
Jimmy Delaney 
In working with Pat, you know, there was Coach Summit, and then there was Pat. And for 
some of us, we were lucky to see both of those and how they wove into each other. 
And the one thing that it's still, even now as a unit head and here at the athletic department 
kind of coming up, the phrase, you win in life with people. And so, as I think about all of the 
Definite Dozen and the things we've talked about: 
• Communicate 
• Leadership 
• Loyalty 
All of that, it really speaks to you win in life with people. And Pat not only said it, you saw 
her do it every day and you felt it as someone that was in that circle. 
And so whether it was, you know, driving her to an appearance or trying to take a game or 
game atmosphere to another level or planning a championship celebration, whatever it 
might have been, Pat was always as invested in you as you were invested in what was going 
on. 
And so, I think still to this day, professionally, personally, everything, like when you talk 
about winning in life with people, that truly is it.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 9: Pat Sings Rocky Top 
Jimmy Delaney 
When Pat was coaching, it was mid to late 2000s, and the men's basketball coach that was 
here, you know, kind of did some crazy antics and all of that, and painted his chest and came to 
a game. And national news and great support and the fans loved it and all of that. 
And so, Pat was sitting there and she was like, well, I need to do something for a men's 
basketball game. And what is it that I can do? And I wanted to be kind of something wild and 
fun and crazy. And so we were sitting around the table, Dean Lockwood and Holly and Nikki and 
a few of us were all just trying to throw out ideas and this and that. 
And what a lot of folks may or may not realize, Pat, you know, she never said she had the 
greatest singing voice, but she loved Rocky Top and she loved singing Rocky Top. And so 
whether, you know, she was having a dinner at her house or, you know, speaking engagement, 
whatever it was, at some point she kind of would work in breaking into Rocky Top. 
And so we're like, Pat, what if you go out and you sing Rocky Top? And she's like, well, I can do 
that, but is that enough? Like he painted his chest. And so we started talking more and we're 
like, well, what if we kind of did it under the slight of hand and, you know, we have all the 
cheerleaders kind of crowd around you and you just hear this voice. And it might take people a 
second to recognize the voice or whatever it is, but you're kind of singing and all of that. 
And then we're like, what if you guys dressed up as cheerleaders? And there was about 30 
seconds of silence in the room. And I was like, okay, so that's the bad idea and I'm never going 
to be invited to a brainstorm again. And she looked at me and she goes, you can get us 
cheerleader uniforms that'll fit all of us? And I was like, sure we can. 
And she was like, all right, so I run off, get with the cheer coach, get the uniforms, bring them 
back in, lay them on the table a day or two later. And everyone comes in and Pat's like, all right, 
we're doing this. And there was about five to 10 minutes of laughter because I think at that 
point in their career and their life, they had never imagined that they'd be wearing a 
cheerleading uniform. Dean Lockwood probably was my favorite because the minute he put on 
the top and the pants, he immediately started going into the arm pumping and all of that. 
But we got the entire coaching staff, Pat included, dressed up in cheerleading outfits and 
nobody knew about it. Got them down into the tunnel at the men's game. Peyton Manning 
happened to be at that game, which was kind of even more incredible. Dick Vitale was calling 
the game for TV. And so everything was lining up, a sold-out game and all of that.

And so we go and grab the microphone. We had scripted in the timeout. We didn't tell anybody 
other than the cheerleaders that were surrounding them like, hey, the start of this timeout, it's 
just going to be a bit where the cheerleaders come out. And we're standing back there. 
And I remember Pat said, she goes, “How do I look?” And I said, “Ridiculous, but you go on in 30 
seconds.” And so, she grabbed the mic and she said, “Is this thing on?” I said, “Oh, it's on.” And 
so the timeout happens, and the cheerleaders crowd around her, and she starts into the “Wish 
that I was...” and the place immediately goes nuts. And I don't know that I've heard Thompson 
Bowling Arena louder. And then they make a pyramid, and they put Pat at the top. And that 
was one of like the lasting images I have.

If you don’t have confidence in your current employee base and overall hiring processes to find good people, that’s the first place to start. But let’s assume that you do — that your human resources team is doing a good job of finding quality employees to fit open roles. How do you start showing loyalty to people you’ve hired?

Loyalty is a self-less proposition. You won’t ever have it unless you’re willing to give it away first.”

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 10: How to Be Loyal to Your Team 
Petra Dunn 
Do you have your employees back? That question could be taken several different ways. Do you 
mean in a disagreement? With benefits? Or in areas of promotion? In a word, yes. As Pat once 
said, loyalty is something that must be tended to on a daily basis. It's a bond that must continue 
to be strengthened throughout the inevitable highs and lows. 
But what does that mean specifically? In this lesson, we'll look at some specific ways you can 
champion your own team members. Think about the last time someone showed you loyalty in a 
troubled spot. What if you could recreate that feeling in the workplace? Loyalty is something 
that is caught more than taught, as they say. It's something team members have to feel or 
experience for themselves, not just something you can verbally tell them is important. 
The good news is there are several ways you can begin to show intentional loyalty to your team 
members. Loyalty can be shown with great benefits, yes. Who doesn't appreciate a great 
compensation package? But that's not the only way. And it's becoming harder and harder to 
stand out in the workplace solely with good benefits. We're talking about the unique loyalty 
you as a leader can model and pass on to your team. 
For example: 
Viewing everyone as a star player. As Pat once put it, “If you seek out quality people and 
convince them to be loyal to your organization, you will succeed, but you must be willing to 
acknowledge their talents and let them do their jobs.” This means giving them a level of trust 
from the beginning as part of the team, not making trust something that starts on zero and has 
to be earned. 
Championing team member growth. Pat did this excellently. She knew how to take 
underdeveloped, bright young athletes and give them increasing responsibilities. The pathways 
for growth on her team were clearly outlined. It wasn't a mystery. Team member growth 
should be a priority, not an afterthought when it comes to cultivating loyal employees. This 
means being slow to offboard or not overreacting to people's mistakes. Conflicts are going to 
happen. Mistakes are going to be made. Those times will test your loyalty to your team 
members. Do you cut the rope and turn them loose? Or do you give them a reasonable time to 
work on their behavior and correct? Nothing kills loyalty among team members more than 
watching other team members be axed or terminated for little to no reason. 
Finally, recognize your rock stars. This means celebrating wins and looking to catch people 
doing the right things. The best leaders know to not only do this, but how to do it well. You also

want to look for ways to cultivate an environment where team members are loyal to each 
other. 
For example: 
Communicate openly about company goals, challenges, and decisions, creating an environment 
where employees feel informed and included. When everyone has equal access to the 
information, it eliminates unnecessary rivalries and pecking orders. 
Hold regular team meetings where employees are encouraged to voice their opinions. This 
keeps things from being bottled and leaking into the gossip mill. It also prevents one employee 
from having the ear of senior leadership and everyone else feels excluded. 
Follow through on your promises. When leaders follow through on their promises, it sets a 
standard for the entire team. Clearly communicate job duties and roles among the team. 
Nothing creates contention and disloyalty faster than confusion among who is doing what. If 
someone has authority in a particular area, make sure the team knows it, rather than refusing 
to clarify. This can lead to team members thinking leadership has a teacher's pet and can cause 
disloyalty among your team. 
When conflict arises between team members, encourage them to work it out first between 
themselves before calling in upper management. This puts the responsibility on them for their 
own interactions and relationships with their team members without leveraging leadership as a 
referee. 
These are just a few things you can do to not only be loyal to your team, but encourage them to 
be loyal to each other.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
If showing loyalty is the first step to growing loyalty, it’s worth taking a step back to examine your current organizational culture. Take a moment to pause and reflect: If you were one of your team members, would you feel like the company is loyal to you? How loyal on a scale of 1 to 10?

If you don’t have confidence in your current employee base and overall hiring processes to find good people, that’s the first place to start. But let’s assume that you do — that your human resources team is doing a good job of finding quality employees to fit open roles. How do you start showing loyalty to people you’ve hired?

items.name: — Pat Summitt
items.paragraph: Loyalty is a self-less proposition. You won’t ever have it unless you’re willing to give it away first.”

Lesson 2 of 8
Everyone a Star

Scroll through to complete this element.

Everyone a Star

The simplest way to show loyalty is to start by letting people do their jobs. In other words, a certain level of trust comes with the job. The message is clear: “We hired you. We believe in you.”
This sounds obvious, but many well-meaning organizations are crippled by inadvertent traditions of micromanagement or unreasonable expectations of seniority.
Let’s look at a few examples of what this can look like.

Summary

There are nuances to every story, but the one thing all these examples have in common is that the companies who hired Tyson, Shelby, and Juan didn’t have much initial loyalty to them as they tried to perform in their roles. There’s an old saying, “See everyone as a star.” In the workplace, this means remembering why you hired someone and looking for the ways they shine. It means celebrating what makes them unique, rather than trying to force them into the mold of their counterparts or predecessors.
Pat asked herself, What do my athletes need to deliver? So, ask yourself: What do my employees need to deliver in their roles?, How can I help?, and sometimes, How can I get out of their way?

Tyson

Let’s say Tyson, a highly skilled, associate-level marketer, has been hired  to create a marketing funnel for a new division of the company. The problem is, the director of marketing doesn’t really trust Tyson to execute.
Tyson patiently sits in meeting after meeting while the director explains what he would do. Tyson tries his best to follow through, including giving a few additional ideas that are new and innovative. The marketing director sends them to the board of directors for review, but they’re quickly shot down in an email. Six months later, Tyson is still struggling to build a funnel that will appease everyone. Tyson was hired to do a specific job, but the very people who hired him don’t show much loyalty to the expertise they hired him for. After 10 more months, he gets frustrated and quits.

Shelby

In another example, Shelby has been working as an entry-level graphic designer for three years, eagerly accepting every new project and working on improving the company’s brand standards. She helps her colleagues out consistently and is always willing to take on extra work. Her designs are well-received by stakeholders and have improved the customer experience on the website dramatically.
When it comes time to hire an associate design director, the company looks at outside candidates, settling on someone the same age and skill level as Shelby but who came highly recommended from a competitor. Shelby is crushed. It will be years until the department is big enough to hire another associate design director. She quietly starts putting in resumes elsewhere.

Juan

Juan is a highly sought-after product manager with 10 years of experience. He joins a company looking to take their existing line of products to the next level and expand into two new markets. The problem is, Juan is consistently left out of key conversations about the product by the C-suite team. They meet regularly to discuss the gaps and flaws in the current product, telling Juan what they would like him to do about it.
When Juan does manage to get invited to a meeting and share his thoughts, he’s told: “When you’ve been here at least five years, your opinion will count more.” Juan doesn’t want to wait five years to have a voice in his own role. When a recruiter calls two months later, he accepts a similar role at another company.

Exercise

Which of these behaviors shows loyalty to your team, versus disloyalty?
Drag and drop each card to complete this element.

Promoting from within

Excessive feedback and approval loops

Telling team members how to perform their job duties

Trusting team members who are subject matter experts

Having your employees’ back during both success and failure

Hiring from the outside, when qualified internal candidates exist

Encouraging a culture of experimentation, without retribution

Leaving junior-level team members out of important discussions

Finger-pointing when things fail

Asking those you manage, “How can I help you?”

Only listening to senior-level management

Clear communication across all position-levels

Clarifying the goals and trusting team members to deliver

Loyalty

Disloyalty

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 3 of 8
Championing Team Member Growth

Heading

The second step in showing loyalty is a fairly obvious one: To show loyalty to your team, you have to invest in the growth of your team members. What does this look like specifically? For Pat and her players, it started with increasing levels of responsibility, as we discussed in the previous module on Responsibility. For your organization, it may mean delegating freely and giving team members a chance to increase their influence or responsibilities in their current roles, before being promoted.

Many times, this involves providing training and continuing education opportunities on the job to help people grow in their skills. A person who is on the cutting edge of a particular industry will quickly grow stale five to eight years later (through no character flaw of their own) if not given the opportunity to further their skills and stay current with the latest trends and technology. Don’t inadvertently punish talented and loyal employees for staying at your company for years by hiring someone from the outside solely because they know the latest trends. Give current employees the opportunity to further their skills on the job.

A large part of employee growth is providing opportunities for advancement. As we saw in Shelby’s example, nothing erodes loyalty faster than competent employees who have been with the company for several years being passed over for internal positions. Internal promotions may not always be feasible, but it’s worth taking a firm look at what the career paths are for your current employees. First, decide if ample opportunities exist. Then look around your own department or ask your HR team for what percentage of promotions are being hired externally and what percentage are being promoted from within — are those opportunities being realized?

Lesson 5 of 8
Recognizing Your Stars

Being Slow to Offboard

OK, that’s all fine when you’ve got employees who are great at their jobs, you might think. But when you’ve worked hard to get an employee hired, and it’s not quite working out in a particular role, what do you do? Many employers simply cut their losses and move on. Employees are expendable, right? Not so fast!

If an employee is a good culture fit, it’s worth examining whether there might be another role that would be a better fit before jumping straight to a termination plan. As Pat would say, you’ve got to get people “in the right seat on the bus.” Being quick to promote and slow to offboard shows employees that the company is committed to them and will make every effort to ensure they can have a career at the organization.

Recognizing Your Rock Stars

No matter what their seat on the bus, a little recognition toward your employees goes a long way. The best companies know not only how to do this, but also how to do it well.
There are many different ways to recognize team members for excelling in their roles. Here are a few ideas.
Please click each to complete this element.

Verbal Praise and Appreciation

One of the simplest yet most effective ways is through sincere verbal praise. Acknowledge their accomplishments and express gratitude for their efforts.

Public Recognition

Publicly recognizing employees' achievements during team meetings, company-wide announcements, or newsletters can amplify the recognition… and inspire others to strive for excellence as well.

Written Recognition

It sounds traditional, but a handwritten note, an email, or a personalized message can have a significant impact. Some people keep cards of appreciation at their desk for years! Seize the opportunity to provide detailed feedback, and express appreciation in writing.

Awards

To standardize recognition efforts, many companies choose to institute a series of weekly, monthly or annual awards to recognize outstanding achievement in a certain area.

Reward Programs

Consider implementing reward programs that provide tangible incentives for exceptional performance. These can include gift cards, bonuses, extra time off or other rewards.

Peer-to-Peer Recognition

Encourage a culture of peer-to-peer recognition where employees can acknowledge and appreciate each other's contributions.

Celebrate Ordinary Accomplishments

Organize celebrations to mark significant milestones, project completions or team successes. Birthdays or company anniversaries are a start. These events can be formal or informal, such as team lunches and happy hours.

Heading

With just a little intentionality, you can make your team members feel valued and appreciated on a regular basis.

If an employee is a good culture fit, it’s worth examining whether there might be another role that would be a better fit before jumping straight to a termination plan. As Pat would say, you’ve got to get people “in the right seat on the bus.” Being quick to promote and slow to offboard shows employees that the company is committed to them and will make every effort to ensure they can have a career at the organization.

No matter what their seat on the bus, a little recognition toward your employees goes a long way. The best companies know not only how to do this, but also how to do it well.
There are many different ways to recognize team members for excelling in their roles. Here are a few ideas.
Please click each to complete this element.

items: One of the simplest yet most effective ways is through sincere verbal praise. Acknowledge their accomplishments and express gratitude for their efforts.
Public Recognition
Publicly recognizing employees' achievements during team meetings, company-wide announcements, or newsletters can amplify the recognition… and inspire others to strive for excellence as well.
Written Recognition

It sounds traditional, but a handwritten note, an email, or a personalized message can have a significant impact. Some people keep cards of appreciation at their desk for years! Seize the opportunity to provide detailed feedback, and express appreciation in writing.
Awards
To standardize recognition efforts, many companies choose to institute a series of weekly, monthly or annual awards to recognize outstanding achievement in a certain area.
Reward Programs
Consider implementing reward programs that provide tangible incentives for exceptional performance. These can include gift cards, bonuses, extra time off or other rewards.
Peer-to-Peer Recognition
Encourage a culture of peer-to-peer recognition where employees can acknowledge and appreciate each other's contributions.
Celebrate Ordinary Accomplishments

Organize celebrations to mark significant milestones, project completions or team successes. Birthdays or company anniversaries are a start. These events can be formal or informal, such as team lunches and happy hours.
With just a little intentionality, you can make your team members feel valued and appreciated on a regular basis.

Lesson 7 of 8
Showing Loyalty With Benefits

Heading

Finally, take a step back and reflect on whether your organization’s compensation/benefits say “loyalty,” or “bare minimum.” The fact is, it’s hard to be loyal to a company whose benefits don’t encourage long-term careers. A few of the key areas include:
(Please click each to complete this element)

Do employees have to show outstanding performance, just get what equates to a cost-of-living raise, or is there room for outstanding compensation?

Healthy pay increases

Otherwise known as “you do good work for us, we’ll let you rest."

PTO/Sick time

This can include dental, vision, life insurance, disability, long-term care, etc.

Health benefits

This says, “We value you, and you won’t have to leave to be able to save well for retirement.” Consider adding a company match.

Retirement plans

It sounds like a no-brainer, but very few businesses manage to do all of the above. Some only do two or three and try to make up for a deficiency in one area by giving away free sports tickets or adding a gym plan. Such perks are appreciated – but do not mistake the small things for big things. Employees won’t work for a company with subpar health insurance simply because they get a discount on live event tickets.

Your company benefits may or may not be directly up to you as a leader, but as a member of the leadership team, encourage upper management to consistently reevaluate what’s being offered and how to show employees that the company is dedicated to their long-term growth.
By championing your team members, publicly recognizing them, encouraging their growth, and providing first-class benefits, you’ll cultivate a culture of loyalty that’s hard to beat.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 11: How to Be a Leader No One Will Want to Leave 
Nikki Fargas 
Have you ever had a leader you would do anything for? Sometimes we like to make loyalty out 
to be a complicated, mythical element. In reality, it all comes down to one basic principle: trust. 
Mutual trust between an employer and a team member modeled first by the leader. 
There are five basic principles of creating trust that we'll go over in the following lesson: 
• Trust is automatically assumed. 
• Team members are defended. 
• Team members are allowed to do their jobs. 
• Team members are allowed to give feedback. 
• Good stewards are rewarded. 
These five elements are a great place to start in establishing yourself as a leader no one will 
want to leave. In other words, world's greatest boss. Pat herself was quick to point out the 
merits of these principles and model them for her athletes. We all struggle in different areas. 
And as we go over the five principles in the lesson below, think about where you fall in these 
five. 
Pat taught us that teamwork is really a form of trust. She said that when that happens, you 
surrender the mistaken idea that you can go at this alone. But you realize that you won't 
achieve your individual goals without the support of your colleagues. Pat also taught us that 
trust allows individuals to feel safe, supported, and respected, leading to a deeper connection 
and a better collaboration. Investing time and effort in building trust can lead to long-lasting, 
fulfilling relationships built on mutual understanding and respect. 
As a young coach, Pat trusted me. We were playing in the SEC tournament for a championship. 
And we were down by one point, and coach trusted my scouting judgment against the team 
that we were playing against. I opted to foul immediately to give us more time to go down and 
call a play. So she hands me the clipboard. So we put the ball in our best player's hand, Candace 
Parker at this time. And we call 1-4 flat, which was also known as Virginia. And we actually got 
this play from the University of Virginia under the legendary coach Debbie Ryan. The 1-4 flat 
play, we drew it up, we came down, we missed the layup, another player came in, she was able 
to put the layup back in, and we were able to win a victory. But I want to say thank you, coach, 
for trusting me.

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 2 of 4
Building Trust

Scroll through to complete this element.

How to Build Trust

When it comes to loyalty, the first thing a leader can do is create a culture of trust.
There are five basic principles to creating a culture of trust:
Trust is automatically assumed.
Team members are defended.
Team members are allowed to do their jobs.
Team members are allowed to give feedback.
Good stewards are rewarded.
Let’s look at each of these in a little more detail.

Conclusion

By putting these principles into action, you too can be a leader no one will ever want to leave.

Trust is automatically assumed.

Assuming you’re hiring adults over the age of 21, everyone who works for your company is essentially an adult. And not just any adult — an adult with a sought-after skill. Otherwise, they wouldn’t be working at your great organization, right? You’d be surprised at how often leaders fail to recognize this, treating employees like they’re teenagers looking for any excuse to misbehave when the boss turns their head. Team members pick up on a vibe of management distrust quicker than almost anything. Most of the time they don’t have to imagine it — it’s outlined in a dense set of departmental rules aimed at the lowest common denominator.
This distrust is the first layer of loyalty that threatens to unravel. Ask any employee and they’ll tell you it’s hard to be loyal to an organization that doesn’t trust you to be on time, avoid gossip, work throughout the workday, communicate clearly, adhere to deadlines, etc. Truth be told, you may have 20 highly skilled, high-functioning employees, and two that you… well, have to keep an eye on. But we humbly recommend dealing with discipline violations or performance pitfalls individually, not with blanket policy or a culture of intense scrutiny. A certain amount of trust should be assumed upon hire, not “earned.”

Team members are defended.

Part of being loyal to people is defending them in public and disciplining them in private. Any parent with children has probably seen this principle play out over and over. It’s no different in a work family. When a team member makes a visible mistake, are they chastised publicly for it? If someone criticizes one of your employees, are you quick to join in, or do you defend the team member? Even the most loyal team member will waver if they learn they will be publicly crucified when they make a mistake. After all, it’s hard to show loyalty to someone who won’t be loyal to you when it counts.

Team members are allowed to do their job.

We talked about this briefly in the previous lesson, but it’s worth stating again. Pat advised, “If you are both strong and selective, if you seek out quality people and convince them to be loyal to your organization, then you will succeed, and you will eliminate a lot of trouble, mistakes and wasted energy along the way. But you must be willing to acknowledge their talents and let them do their jobs.”1

Team members are allowed to give feedback.

A lack of feedback always keeps a relationship one-sided. It takes a certain level of maturity and trust to be prepared for whatever that feedback might be. But the highest-functioning teams have a high level of trust that allows for feedback to be given when necessary — for the overall good of the team or organization.
Pat put it this way: “When I say surround yourself with loyal people, I don’t mean ‘yes people.’ I want to make that clear. In fact, it’s a crucial distinction… You have to allow for differences and entertain the opinions of others, without accusing them of disloyalty.”
“People who say yes to you all the time are, in my opinion, insulting you. They assume you are either too immature or unstable or egotistical to handle the truth,” she said.
Employees must have a safe place to voice their concerns and give feedback so they feel like they’re part of a team.
Note: A key distinction here is “feedback,” not “complaints.” Assuming the feedback is constructive and given in the right spirit, never criticize an employee for giving feedback when it’s been encouraged or solicited.

Good stewards are rewarded.

Nothing increases loyalty like rewarding competent people for a job well done. When team members see a direct relationship between work and reward, it makes them more motivated and more loyal to an organization.
With a little intentionality, you can use the steps above to help lay a foundation of trust as a leader. Think back on the best leaders you’ve had over the course of your own career. What made them so great? Most likely, the common denominator was that you felt like they trusted you. They earned your loyalty by first giving you trust and/or loyalty in return.

Joan Cronan 
You know, when I think about loyalty and Pat Summitt, unfortunately, as you know, we lost Pat

there at the celebration of life.

Lesson 1 of 1
The Power of Team Wrap-Up

(Download the transcript below)

Heading

In today’s ever-evolving landscape, success is often seen as an individual achievement. However, the age-old wisdom, "If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together," reminds us of the enduring power of a cohesive team. The dynamics of a team are fueled by responsibility, communication, and loyalty — three pillars that not only fortify the team structure, but also pave the way for group success.

Imagine a team as a chain, where each link represents an individual team member. When the links are strong and interconnected, the chain becomes unbreakable. In contrast, a weak link jeopardizes the integrity of the entire structure.
(Scroll through to complete this element)

Reflect

Now that we’ve discussed how some of these can help your team, consider how you can put these three principles into practice with those you lead.

Responsibility

As discussed, responsibility goes beyond individual tasks. It’s about a collective commitment to the team's goals and objectives. Each team member plays a crucial role in the success of the team, and a strong sense of responsibility ensures that everyone is accountable for their actions.
A responsible team is one where each member understands their role, takes ownership of their tasks, and contributes to the overall success of the team. This creates an environment where challenges are faced head-on, and setbacks become opportunities for learning and improvement.

Communication

Effective communication is the lifeblood of any successful team. It involves more than just conveying information; it’s about understanding, collaboration, and creating an atmosphere where ideas can flow freely. Teams that communicate well take advantage of the collective intelligence of their members, resulting in innovative solutions and championship-level performance.

Loyalty

Last but not least, a shared sense of loyalty to each other and an organization fosters a sense of unity, trust, and camaraderie among team members. Loyalty within a team is not blind allegiance but a deep commitment to the shared goals and values. It’s the glue that holds a team together during challenging times and propels them toward shared successes.

The Tools for a Winning Team

In the pursuit of success, the power of team cannot be overstated. The combination of responsibility, communication, and loyalty creates a formidable force capable of extraordinary accomplishments. As individuals, we may have unique strengths, but it is within the framework of a team that these strengths can be magnified to their full potential.
As we navigate the workforce, from now on embrace “the power of team,” understanding that together, we can not only achieve our goals, but also go far beyond what we could ever imagine on our own!

“Teamwork is what makes common people capable of uncommon results.”

Click play to hear the quote above.

Congratulations!

If you want to go far, go together," reminds us of the enduring power of a cohesive team. The dynamics of a team are fueled by responsibility, communication, and loyalty — three pillars that not only fortify the team structure, but also pave the way for group success.

body_blocks.text:
Imagine a team as a chain, where each link represents an individual team member. When the links are strong and interconnected, the chain becomes unbreakable. In contrast, a weak link jeopardizes the integrity of the entire structure.
(Scroll through to complete this element)
items: Reflect
Now that we’ve discussed how some of these can help your team, consider how you can put these three principles into practice with those you lead.
Responsibility

As discussed, responsibility goes beyond individual tasks. It’s about a collective commitment to the team's goals and objectives. Each team member plays a crucial role in the success of the team, and a strong sense of responsibility ensures that everyone is accountable for their actions.
A responsible team is one where each member understands their role, takes ownership of their tasks, and contributes to the overall success of the team. This creates an environment where challenges are faced head-on, and setbacks become opportunities for learning and improvement.
Communication

Effective communication is the lifeblood of any successful team. It involves more than just conveying information; it’s about understanding, collaboration, and creating an atmosphere where ideas can flow freely. Teams that communicate well take advantage of the collective intelligence of their members, resulting in innovative solutions and championship-level performance.
Loyalty

Last but not least, a shared sense of loyalty to each other and an organization fosters a sense of unity, trust, and camaraderie among team members. Loyalty within a team is not blind allegiance but a deep commitment to the shared goals and values. It’s the glue that holds a team together during challenging times and propels them toward shared successes.

body_blocks.text: The Tools for a Winning Team

In the pursuit of success, the power of team cannot be overstated. The combination of responsibility, communication, and loyalty creates a formidable force capable of extraordinary accomplishments. As individuals, we may have unique strengths, but it is within the framework of a team that these strengths can be magnified to their full potential.
As we navigate the workforce, from now on embrace “the power of team,” understanding that together, we can not only achieve our goals, but also go far beyond what we could ever imagine on our own!
“Teamwork is what makes common people capable of uncommon results.”
Click play to hear the quote above.

Congratulations!
That concludes this course. Please remember to close it before opening another course. You can revisit the completed course material at any time.

video.transcript_text:
Conclusion: The Power of Team 
Corinne Milien 
So, to wrap it up, we've talked about how responsibility, loyalty, and communication are 
the foundation of successful teams. Take a moment to think about where your team is and 
how you can start to implement some of these principles. Being a part of an amazing team 
is something you'll never forget. It doesn't come naturally, but it can be taught. 
When people understand their roles and trust their teammates to do their job, like I've 
witnessed on multiple SEC championships for the Lady Vols, it was amazing. We had: 
Shooters who shot, people who grabbed rebounds, ladies to make defensive plays. 
Everyone knew their role. It helped us win games. In her book, Reach for the Summit, Pat 
said, "You don't just lump a group of people together in a room and call them a team and 
expect them to behave like one. No organization will succeed without teamwork, no matter 
how many all-stars you have." 
“I talk about teamwork until I have no voice left. Without an incentive, people simply won't 
work together consistently. But if you grasp the real incentive behind teamwork, it 
suddenly becomes a whole lot easier. Teamwork is really just a form of trust. It's what 
happens when you surrender the mistaken idea that you can go at it alone and realize that 
you won't achieve your personal goals without the support of your colleagues. Once you 
buy into it, you'll feel a sense of relief. It's like relaxing into a chair after a long day on your 
feet.” 
At the end of the day, you play a major part in creating a team that no one will want to 
leave, a team that makes going into work a joy, a team that makes reaching difficult 
obstacles easy, maybe even fun. I was the person in the office when the players needed a 
snack or they needed a laugh, they knew where to go. Me. It seemed small, but that outlet 
played a big part in their well-being off the court. 
I knew my strengths and I felt empowered by the coaches, players, and staff to bring my 
authentic self to the office every day because that's what the team needed. So you go out 
there and make these principles your own. You have the tools to make your career and 
your organization great. We're right behind you all the way and we're cheering you on.
